orig_cross_topic_revision_algebra_functi.description: Choose a useful quadratic form, keep the original domains visible, and turn algebraic roots into solutions that really belong to the problem.

sections.title: Which quadratic form makes the next step easier?
sections.label: Choose a useful form
sections.intro: Start with what the question asks. Rewriting a quadratic can reveal the answer more clearly than expanding every expression at once.

blocks.html:
• Standard form \(ax^2+bx+c\) identifies the coefficients for a formula or discriminant.
  • Factorised form \(a(x-r_1)(x-r_2)\), when available over the reals, reveals roots and signs.
  • Completed-square form \(a(x-h)^2+k\) reveals the vertex \((h,k)\), the range and a possible inverse branch.

For a genuine quadratic, \(a\ne0\). When completing the square, factor \(a\) out of the quadratic and linear terms without changing the function’s scale.

blocks.title: Choose a form that reveals the required information
blocks.prompt: For \(q(x)=x^2+4x-5\), find its roots and minimum value. Then choose the interval on which \(q(x)\le0\).
blocks.hint: Factorise to locate the roots and complete the square to find the minimum. The coefficient of \(x^2\) is positive.
blocks.solution:
1. \[q(x)=(x+5)(x-1)=(x+2)^2-9.\]

  2. The roots are \(-5\) and \(1\). The minimum is \(-9\), attained at \(x=-2\).

  3. The upward-opening parabola is on or below the axis between its roots. Therefore \(-5\le x\le1\), including both endpoints.

blocks.html: For an inequality, find where the expression has the required sign and include endpoints only when equality is allowed. Intersect that interval with any domain supplied in the question.

sections.title: How does the original domain choose the inverse?
sections.label: Range and inverse branch
sections.intro: A function needs to be one-to-one to have an inverse on its full range. A complete parabola fails this test, but a suitable restricted branch can pass it. Complete the square and identify the actual range before rearranging.

blocks.html:
From \(y=a(x-h)^2+k\), with \(a\ne0\),

\[x=h\pm\sqrt{\frac{y-k}{a}}.\]

Choose the sign that returns inputs in the original domain. The original range becomes the inverse domain, and the original domain becomes the inverse range. Strict endpoints stay strict.

1. On the restricted branch, \(f(x)=(x-1)^2+2\) and \(x\ge1\).
  2. Solving \(f(x)=6\) gives \((x-1)^2=4\) and \(x=-1,3\). The allowed solution is \(x=3\).
  3. For \(k>2\), only \(x=1+\sqrt{k-2}\) remains. At \(k=2\) the endpoint \(x=1\) is included. A level with \(k<2\) does not meet the curve.

The line \(y=6\) meets the full parabola at \(x=-1\) and \(x=3\), but the domain \(x\ge1\) retains only \(3\).

blocks.title: A left branch and a strict endpoint change the inverse
blocks.prompt: Let \(g(x)=(x+3)^2-1\), with domain \(x<-3\). Select its inverse formula and inverse domain, then find \(g^{-1}(8)\).
blocks.hint: The original inputs satisfy \(x+3<0\), so choose the negative square-root branch. The vertex is excluded.
blocks.solution:
1. On \(x<-3\), the output satisfies \(g(x)>-1\), and every value above \(-1\) occurs.

  2. \[y+1=(x+3)^2,\qquad x+3=-\sqrt{y+1}.\]
  3. \[g^{-1}(x)=-3-\sqrt{x+1},\qquad x>-1.\]
  4. \[g^{-1}(8)=-3-3=-6.\]

    The value \(-6\) belongs to the original domain, and \(g(-6)=8\).

blocks.html:
1. The restricted function maps \([1,\infty)\to[2,\infty)\). Its inverse maps \([2,\infty)\to[1,\infty)\).
  2. Swap inputs and outputs. From \(x=(y-1)^2+2\) and \(y\ge1\), keep \(y=1+\sqrt{x-2}\).
  3. For example, \(f^{-1}(6)=3\) and \(f^{-1}(2)=1\). The endpoint \((1,2)\) becomes \((2,1)\) under reflection.

The allowed point \((3,6)\) reflects to \((6,3)\) in the inverse graph. The included endpoint \((1,2)\) reflects to the included endpoint \((2,1)\).

An inverse is not a reciprocal: \(f^{-1}(x)\) does not mean \(\frac{1}{f(x)}\). The inverse identities also have domains:

\[f^{-1}(f(x))=x\quad\text{for }x\in\operatorname{Dom}(f),\]\[f(f^{-1}(y))=y\quad\text{for }y\in\operatorname{Range}(f).\]

sections.title: Which inputs are allowed in a composite function?
sections.label: Check both functions
sections.intro: In \(f(g(x))\), apply \(g\) first. The original input must be allowed by \(g\), and its output must be an allowed input for \(f\). Reversing the order usually changes both the expression and its domain.

blocks.html:
\[\operatorname{Dom}(f\circ g)=\{x\in\operatorname{Dom}(g):g(x)\in\operatorname{Dom}(f)\}.\]

Check nonnegative square-root inputs, nonzero denominators and any stated branch restriction. If the composition is required on the whole supplied domain of \(g\), its entire range must lie in the domain of \(f\); otherwise state the needed input restriction.

blocks.title: The inner rational output must be allowed by the square root
blocks.prompt: Let \(f(u)=\sqrt{u}\) and \(g(x)=\frac{x+1}{x-2}\), each with its natural real domain. Choose the allowed domain of \(f(g(x))\), then solve \(f(g(x))=2\).
blocks.hint: The denominator must be nonzero and the complete rational expression under the root must be nonnegative. Test signs around \(-1\) and \(2\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[x\ne2,\qquad\frac{x+1}{x-2}\ge0.\]

  2. The quotient is nonnegative for \(x\le-1\) or \(x>2\). At \(-1\) it is zero; at \(2\) it is undefined.

  3. \[\frac{x+1}{x-2}=4\Longrightarrow x+1=4x-8\Longrightarrow x=3.\]

  4. This input belongs to the composite domain, and the original square root is \(\sqrt{4}=2\).

blocks.html: Write the composite domain before solving its equation or inequality. For example, a restriction \(u\ge h\) on the outer function becomes \(g(x)\ge h\), not automatically \(x\ge h\).

sections.title: Which algebraic roots solve the original problem?
sections.label: Check every possible solution
sections.intro: An algebraic step can enlarge the set of possible answers. Squaring hides signs, clearing denominators can admit excluded inputs, and cancelling a factor can hide a hole. Keep the original restrictions beside the calculation.

blocks.html: For \(\sqrt{A(x)}=B(x)\), require both \(A(x)\ge0\) and \(B(x)\ge0\) before using \(A(x)=B(x)^2\). Then check the resulting values in the original equation.

blocks.title: Cancellation does not restore an excluded input
blocks.prompt: Solve \(\frac{x^2-4}{x-2}=4\). Give the algebraic value obtained after cancellation and the final solution set for the original equation.
blocks.hint: Record the denominator restriction before cancelling \(x-2\). Check whether the resulting value satisfies it.
blocks.solution:
1. \[x\ne2,\qquad\frac{(x-2)(x+2)}{x-2}=x+2\quad\text{only for }x\ne2.\]
  2. \[x+2=4\Longrightarrow x=2.\]

  3. That input is excluded from the original equation, so there are no solutions. The final solution set is \(\varnothing\).

blocks.html: Do not divide by an expression that might be zero without considering that case separately. A cancelled denominator remains excluded, while a divided factor can cause a valid zero solution to be lost.

For each possible solution, check the original domain, any sign or interval condition, and the unsimplified equation. A rejected value needs a short reason. If none remain, the original problem has no solution.

sections.title: When does a discriminant count too many intersections?
sections.label: Degree, roots and restrictions
sections.intro: Equate the original graph expressions and collect terms. Before using a quadratic test, check whether a parameter can make the leading coefficient zero. For the genuine quadratic cases, the discriminant counts unrestricted real roots.

blocks.html:
\[ax^2+bx+c=0,\quad a\ne0:\qquad\Delta=b^2-4ac,\]\[x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}.\]

There are two distinct real roots when \(\Delta>0\), one repeated real root when \(\Delta=0\), and none when \(\Delta<0\). Check the resulting inputs against both graph domains afterwards.

blocks.title: A repeated root at a strict boundary is not allowed
blocks.prompt: Consider \(x^2-6x+k=0\) with the restriction \(x>3\). State the number of allowed solutions for \(k=4\), \(k=9\) and \(k=12\). Also give the allowed solution when \(k=4\).
blocks.hint: Rewrite the equation as \((x-3)^2=9-k\), then apply the strict restriction to each root.
blocks.solution:
1. For \(k=4\), the two algebraic roots are \(3\pm\sqrt{5}\). Only \(3+\sqrt{5}\) is greater than \(3\).

  2. For \(k=9\), the repeated root is \(3\), which the domain excludes. There are no allowed solutions.

  3. For \(k=12\), a square would have to equal \(-3\), so there are no real roots at all.

blocks.html: If the leading coefficient vanishes, solve the remaining equation directly. A nonzero linear coefficient gives a linear equation. If both variable coefficients vanish, a true constant statement allows every input in the original domain; a false one allows none.

One allowed intersection need not mean tangency: another real root may be outside the domain. For a claimed tangent, check the repeated contact input and its coordinates in both original graphs. An excluded endpoint is not a contact point.

glossary.definition: A value that satisfies the original equation and every stated restriction.
The set of inputs allowed in the original function.
The set of outputs actually reached on that domain.
Different allowed inputs always produce different outputs.
The choice of inverse expression that returns inputs in the original restricted domain.
A function formed by applying one function to the output of another.
The expression \(b^2-4ac\), used to count real roots when the equation is genuinely quadratic.
An input forbidden by the original domain, even if later algebra hides the reason.

examples.title: Use different forms of the same quadratic
examples.question: Write \(q(x)=2x^2-8x+6\) in factorised and completed-square forms. Use them to find the roots, the minimum and the solution of \(q(x)\le0\).
solution:
Keep the leading factor when completing the square:

\[\begin{aligned}q(x)&=2(x^2-4x)+6\\&=2\bigl((x-2)^2-4\bigr)+6\\&=2(x-2)^2-2.\end{aligned}\]
The minimum is \(-2\), attained at \(x=2\). The vertex is \((2,-2)\).
\[q(x)\le0\Longleftrightarrow(x-2)^2\le1\Longleftrightarrow1\le x\le3.\]
All three expressions define the same function. The useful form depends on whether the question asks for roots, signs or the range.

examples.title: The domain selects one inverse branch
examples.question: Let \(f(x)=(x-1)^2+2\), with domain \(x\ge1\). Find its range and inverse, including the inverse domain. How many allowed solutions does \(f(x)=k\) have?
solution: Since \((x-1)^2\ge0\), and every nonnegative square is reached on this right branch, the range is \([2,\infty)\).

\[y-2=(x-1)^2.\]

The restriction gives \(x-1\ge0\), so

\[x=1+\sqrt{y-2}.\]

\[f^{-1}(x)=1+\sqrt{x-2},\qquad x\ge2.\]

The inverse range is \([1,\infty)\), the original domain.
For \(k<2\), there is no solution. For \(k=2\), the allowed solution is \(x=1\). For \(k>2\), only \(x=1+\sqrt{k-2}\) belongs to the stated domain.
For example, \(k=6\) gives algebraic roots \(-1\) and \(3\), but only \(3\) is allowed. Thus \(f^{-1}(6)=3\).

examples.title: Find the composite domain before solving its equation
examples.question: Let \(f(u)=\frac{1}{u-2}\) and \(g(x)=\sqrt{x+1}\), with their natural real domains. Find the allowed domain of \(f(g(x))\), then solve \(f(g(x))=1\).
solution:
Apply \(g\) first, then \(f\):

\[f(g(x))=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}-2}.\]

The inner square root requires \(x\ge-1\). Its output must also avoid the excluded outer input \(2\):

\[\sqrt{x+1}\ne2\Longrightarrow x\ne3.\]
The allowed domain is \([-1,3)\cup(3,\infty)\).
\[\frac{1}{\sqrt{x+1}-2}=1\Longrightarrow\sqrt{x+1}=3\Longrightarrow x=8.\]
The input \(8\) is allowed, and the original composite gives \(\frac{1}{3-2}=1\). Therefore \(x=8\) is the solution.

examples.title: Check the sign that squaring would hide
examples.question: Solve \(\sqrt{2x+3}=x\) over the real numbers.
solution: The square root requires \(x\ge-\frac{3}{2}\). Its value is nonnegative, so equality also requires \(x\ge0\).
\[2x+3=x^2\Longrightarrow x^2-2x-3=0\Longrightarrow(x-3)(x+1)=0.\]
The algebraic possibilities are \(x=3\) and \(x=-1\). The second fails the required sign condition.
\[x=3:\quad\sqrt{9}=3;\qquad x=-1:\quad\sqrt{1}=1\ne-1.\]
The only solution of the original equation is \(x=3\). Squaring preserved the true solution but also allowed a false one.

examples.title: The discriminant does not finish a restricted intersection count
examples.question: Find the number of intersections of \(y=x^2+4\), restricted to \(x>1\), with \(y=mx\), for every real value of \(m\).
solution:
\[x^2-mx+4=0,\qquad\Delta=m^2-16.\]

At an allowed input, \(m=x+\frac{4}{x}>0\). Combining this with \(\Delta\ge0\) gives \(m\ge4\). There are no allowed intersections for \(m<4\).
When \(m=4\), the equation is \((x-2)^2=0\). Its repeated root \(2\) is allowed, giving one intersection.

For \(m>4\), write \(p(x)=x^2-mx+4\). Its vertex lies at \(x=\frac{m}{2}>2\), its minimum is negative, and

\[p(1)=5-m.\]
If \(4<m<5\), the value at \(1\) is positive. Both roots lie to the right of \(1\), one on each side of the vertex, so both intersections are allowed.

If \(m=5\), the roots are \(1\) and \(4\). The strict boundary excludes \(1\), leaving one intersection. If \(m>5\), then \(p(1)<0\), so \(1\) lies between the two roots and only the larger root is allowed.

\[N(m)=\begin{cases}0,&m<4,\\1,&m=4,\\2,&4<m<5,\\1,&m\ge5.\end{cases}\]

A positive discriminant gives two unrestricted real roots; their locations decide the allowed count.

examples.title: Check whether the equation is still quadratic
examples.question: Classify the number of real solutions of \((k-2)x^2+2x-1=0\) for every real parameter \(k\).
solution:
First check the value that removes the quadratic term. For \(k=2\),

\[2x-1=0\Longrightarrow x=\frac{1}{2}.\]

This is one solution of a linear equation.

For \(k\ne2\), the equation is quadratic, with

\[\Delta=2^2-4(k-2)(-1)=4(k-1).\]
If \(k<1\), there are no real roots. If \(k=1\), the equation is \(-(x-1)^2=0\), giving the repeated root \(1\).

If \(k>1\) and \(k\ne2\), there are two distinct real roots:

\[x=\frac{-1\pm\sqrt{k-1}}{k-2}.\]
Thus the count is zero for \(k<1\), one for \(k=1\) or \(k=2\), and two for \(k>1\), \(k\ne2\). Substituting \(k=2\) into a quadratic formula would be invalid.

extraPractice.title: A completed square fixes the inverse branch
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=2x^2-12x+23\), with domain \(x\le3\). Complete the square, state its range and find its inverse. Enter the vertex, \(f^{-1}(13)\), and the two inclusive endpoints of the solution to \(f(x)\le23\).
extraPractice.hint: The original inputs are on the left of the vertex. The inverse must return an input no greater than \(3\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f(x)=2(x-3)^2+5,\qquad\text{range }[5,\infty).\]
  2. \[f^{-1}(x)=3-\sqrt{\frac{x-5}{2}},\qquad x\ge5.\]
  3. \[f^{-1}(13)=3-\sqrt{4}=1.\]
  4. \[2(x-3)^2+5\le23\Longrightarrow0\le x\le6.\]

  5. Intersect that candidate interval with \(x\le3\). The final solution is \(0\le x\le3\), including both endpoints.

extraPractice.title: Squaring creates a candidate that fails the original equation
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(\sqrt{4-x}=x-2\) over the real numbers. State the allowable interval before squaring, then enter every admissible solution.

retry.feedback: Squaring produced candidates. At \(x=0\), the original right-hand side is negative and cannot equal the principal square root.

extraPractice.hint: The radicand must be nonnegative. The right-hand side must also be nonnegative because it equals a principal square root.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[4-x\ge0,\quad x-2\ge0\Longrightarrow2\le x\le4.\]
  2. \[4-x=(x-2)^2\Longrightarrow x^2-3x=0\Longrightarrow x=0\text{ or }3.\]

  3. The candidate \(0\) is outside the allowable interval and gives \(2=-2\) in the original equation. At \(x=3\), both sides equal \(1\). The solution set is \(\{3\}\).

extraPractice.title: A cancelled denominator still leaves a missing input
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(u)=\frac{1}{u-1}\) and \(g(x)=\frac{x+2}{x-3}\), each on its natural real domain. Simplify \(f(g(x))\), give every excluded input, and solve \(f(g(x))=0\).
extraPractice.hint: First require \(g\) to exist, then require its output to differ from \(1\). Keep these restrictions after simplifying.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[x e3,\qquad g(x)-1= rac{5}{x-3} e0\quad(x e3).\]
  2. \[f(g(x))= rac{1}{ rac{5}{x-3}}= rac{x-3}{5},\qquad x e3.\]

  3. The simplified expression would be zero only at \(x=3\). That input was excluded by the original composition, so there are no solutions.

extraPractice.title: Check whether the equation is still quadratic
extraPractice.prompt: Consider \((k-1)x^2-2kx+k+1=0\). Find the value of \(k\) at which it is not quadratic. For each listed value, give every real solution with \(x\ge0\).

fields.label: Value of k where degree changes

extraPractice.hint: Substitute the value that makes the leading coefficient zero before dividing by it. For the other values, factor the equation and apply \(x\ge0\).
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(k-1)x^2-2kx+k+1=(x-1)\bigl((k-1)x-(k+1)\bigr).\]

  2. At \(k=1\), the equation is \(-2x+2=0\), with the single root \(x=1\).

  3. \[k\ne1:\qquad x=1\quad\text{or}\quad x=\frac{k+1}{k-1}.\]

  4. For \(k=-2\), both \(1\) and \(\frac{1}{3}\) are allowed. For \(k=0\), the second root is \(-1\), which is excluded. For \(k=2\), both \(1\) and \(3\) are allowed.

  5. In the genuine quadratic case the discriminant is \(4\). This guarantees two distinct algebraic real roots, but the restriction can remove one. There are two admissible roots for \(k\le-1\) or \(k>1\), and one for \(-1<k\le1\).

extraPractice.title: An open endpoint can remove the only repeated root
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(f(x)=(x+2)^2-3\), with the strict domain \(x>-2\). Find the number of intersections with each horizontal line \(y=-4\), \(y=-3\) and \(y=1\). For \(y=1\), give the accepted intersection point.

retry.feedback: The repeated root is \(x=-2\), but the strict domain is \(x>-2\). The vertex is excluded.

extraPractice.hint: The vertex lies at an excluded input. A repeated algebraic root is counted only when it belongs to the stated domain.
extraPractice.solution:
1. The range is \((-3,\infty)\). Hence the lines \(y=-4\) and \(y=-3\) have no intersections with this restricted graph.

  2. \[(x+2)^2-3=1\Longrightarrow(x+2)^2=4\Longrightarrow x=0\text{ or }-4.\]

  3. Only \(0>-2\), so the one accepted point is \((0,1)\). The unrestricted parabola would have a vertex at \((-2,-3)\), but that point is absent here.

starters.title: A composite inequality and its inverse use the same branch
starters.question: Let \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+1\), for \(x\ge2\), and \(g(x)=3x-1\), for all real \(x\). Define \(h(x)=f(g(x))\) on the largest real domain where this expression is defined. Find the domain and range of \(h\), solve \(h(x)\le10\), and find \(h^{-1}(17)\). Give the lower bound of the domain, the inclusive endpoints of the inequality solution and the requested inverse value.
starters.hint: Apply the domain of \(f\) to the output of \(g\). On that restricted domain, the expression inside the square is nonnegative.
starters.solution:
1. \[3x-1\ge2\Longrightarrow x\ge1,\qquad h(x)=(3x-3)^2+1.\]

  2. As \(x\) runs through \([1,\infty)\), \(3x-3\) runs through \([0,\infty)\). The range of \(h\) is \([1,\infty)\).

  3. \[(3x-3)^2+1\le10\Longrightarrow-3\le3x-3\le3\Longrightarrow0\le x\le2.\]

  4. Intersect with the domain: \(1\le x\le2\).

  5. \[h^{-1}(y)=1+\frac{\sqrt{y-1}}{3},\qquad y\ge1.\]
  6. \[h^{-1}(17)=1+\frac{4}{3}=\frac{7}{3}.\]

  7. Substitution gives \(g(\frac{7}{3})=6\), an allowed input of \(f\), and \(f(6)=17\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: require the inner output to belong to the outer domain.
  • 1 mark: obtain the simplified composition and its range.
  • 1 mark: solve the squared inequality.
  • 1 mark: intersect with the original domain, retaining both inclusive endpoints.
  • 1 mark: choose the positive branch in the inverse.
  • 1 mark: state the inverse domain.
  • 1 mark: evaluate the inverse and verify its original-domain condition.

starters.title: A discriminant can identify a contact outside the allowed graph
starters.question: The restricted curve is \(y=(x-3)^2\), with \(x\ge3\). A line has equation \(y=mx\). First find every value of \(m\) giving a repeated root of the unrestricted intersection equation. Then identify which of those values gives a contact point on the restricted curve. Find every accepted intersection when \(m=4\), and explain the number of accepted intersections for all real \(m\).
starters.hint: Use the discriminant to find algebraic repeated roots, then check their inputs. On the stated curve \(x\) is positive and \((x-3)^2\) is nonnegative.
starters.solution:
1. \[(x-3)^2=mx\Longrightarrow x^2-(m+6)x+9=0.\]
  2. \[\Delta=(m+6)^2-36=m(m+12)=0\Longrightarrow m=0\text{ or }-12.\]

  3. At \(m=0\), the repeated root is \(x=3\), giving the allowed point \((3,0)\). At \(m=-12\), the repeated root is \(x=-3\), which is excluded.

  4. \[m=4:\qquad x^2-10x+9=(x-1)(x-9)=0.\]

  5. Only \(x=9\) belongs to the domain, so the accepted intersection is \((9,36)\).

  6. If \(m<0\), then \(mx<0\) for \(x\ge3\), while \((x-3)^2\ge0\); no intersection is possible. If \(m=0\), there is the single boundary contact.

  7. If \(m>0\), the quadratic has positive discriminant, its value at \(x=3\) is \(-3m<0\), and its leading coefficient is positive. Thus one root lies below \(3\) and one above \(3\). Exactly one is allowed. The final count is zero for \(m<0\) and one for \(m\ge0\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the intersection equation.
  • 1 mark: calculate and factor the discriminant.
  • 1 mark: obtain both algebraic repeated-root parameter values.
  • 1 mark: check their contact inputs against the restricted domain.
  • 1 mark: solve the equation when the parameter is four.
  • 1 mark: give the accepted coordinate pair only.
  • 1 mark: justify the count for negative and zero parameter values.
  • 1 mark: justify the count for positive parameter values.

revision.body:
Find the algebraic possibilities, then retain only those allowed by the original problem.

Choose the useful quadratic form

Standard form gives coefficients. Factorised form gives roots and signs. Completed-square form \(a(x-h)^2+k\) gives the vertex and helps with ranges and inverses.

Preserve the leading factor. For inequalities, check the sign intervals, the equality endpoints and the stated domain.

Keep the inverse branch and its domain

\[y=a(x-h)^2+k\Longrightarrow x=h\pm\sqrt{\frac{y-k}{a}}.\]

Use the sign required by the original input interval. Swap domain and range, preserving strict endpoints. Inverse identities hold only on their corresponding domains. An inverse is not a reciprocal.

Check composites and algebraic steps

For \(f(g(x))\), require both \(x\in\operatorname{Dom}(g)\) and \(g(x)\in\operatorname{Dom}(f)\). Keep denominator holes after cancellation.

Before squaring \(\sqrt{A}=B\), require \(A\ge0\) and \(B\ge0\). Check every possible value in the original equation. Consider a possible zero factor before dividing by it.

Count allowed intersections

\[a\ne0:\quad\Delta=b^2-4ac,\qquad x=\frac{-b\pm\sqrt{\Delta}}{2a}.\]

Positive, zero and negative discriminants give two, one repeated and no unrestricted real roots. Apply original domains afterwards.

If \(a=0\), solve the remaining equation directly. Check strict boundaries and contact coordinates. One retained root alone does not establish tangency.
revision.checks:
• Useful form chosen without changing the function?
  • Original and composite domains recorded first?
  • Every root checked after squaring, cancellation or division?
  • Degree changes, strict endpoints and contact points checked?

orig_cross_topic_revision_geometry_calcu.description: Combine derivative gradients with perpendicular radii, then use squared distance and the actual domain to justify a nearest point.

sections.title: What information should I collect at a contact point?
sections.label: Point, gradient and radius
sections.intro: Start by checking that the stated point belongs to every original curve involved. A correct gradient at the wrong point cannot establish a tangent. For a circle, identify its centre and ensure that its radius is positive.

blocks.html:
At \(P=(a,f(a))\), with finite derivative \(m=f^{\prime}(a)\), the curve tangent is

\[y-f(a)=m(x-a).\]

When \(m\ne0\), the normal gradient is \(-\frac{1}{m}\). A circle tangent is perpendicular to the radius through its contact point, so the circle centre lies on this normal.

blocks.title: Check the point, then use its local gradient
blocks.prompt: The point \(P=(-1,2)\) lies on \(y=x^2+1\). Write its tangent as \(y=m_Tx+c_T\) and its normal as \(y=m_Nx+c_N\). Find the four coefficients.
blocks.hint: Verify the point height. Use \(f^{\prime}(x)=2x\), then the negative reciprocal for the normal.
blocks.solution:
1. \[(-1)^2+1=2,\qquad m_T=f^{\prime}(-1)=-2.\]
  2. \[y-2=-2(x+1)\Longrightarrow y=-2x.\]
  3. \[m_N=\frac{1}{2},\qquad y-2=\frac{1}{2}(x+1)\Longrightarrow y=\frac{x}{2}+\frac{5}{2}.\]

blocks.html:
1. At \(P=(2,4)\) on \(y=x^2\), \(y'=2x=4\). Thus the tangent is \(y-4=4(x-2)\).
  2. For the circle \((x-6)^2+(y-3)^2=17\), the point gives \(CP^2=(-4)^2+1^2=17\).
  3. The radius gradient is \(-\frac14\), so its product with the line gradient is \(-1\). The line is tangent to both.

At \(P=(2,4)\), the curve tangent has gradient \(4\), while the radius from \(C=(6,3)\) has gradient \(-\frac{1}{4}\). Their common tangent is \(y=4x-4\).

Keep three checks separate: the point is on the original curves, the line passes through that point, and its direction is correct. Substitute into the final line equation as a quick consistency check.

sections.title: How do I confirm or find a circle contact?
sections.label: Geometry and repeated roots
sections.intro: Substitute a line into the circle equation. The resulting quadratic has two distinct real roots for a secant, a repeated root for a tangent and no real roots when the line misses the circle. Recover the point coordinates and check them in the original equations.

blocks.html:
For a circle with centre \((h,k)\), an unknown common contact on \(y=f(x)\) has coordinates \((a,f(a))\). If \(f^{\prime}(a)\ne0\), the normal condition is

\[k-f(a)=-\frac{h-a}{f^{\prime}(a)}.\]

For a horizontal tangent, use the vertical normal \(x=a\) instead. After finding a possible contact, compute \(r^2=(a-h)^2+(f(a)-k)^2\) and verify the original circle conditions.

blocks.title: Use a repeated root to identify circle tangency
blocks.prompt: For the circle \(x^2+y^2=5\), find every value of \(c\) for which \(y=2x+c\) is a tangent. Also find the contact point when \(c=5\).
blocks.hint: Substitute the line into the circle. Tangency gives a repeated root of the resulting quadratic.
blocks.solution:
1. \[x^2+(2x+c)^2=5\Longrightarrow5x^2+4cx+c^2-5=0.\]
  2. \[\Delta=16c^2-20(c^2-5)=4(25-c^2).\]
  3. \[\Delta=0\Longrightarrow c=\pm5.\]

  4. For \(c=5\), the equation becomes \(5(x+2)^2=0\), so \(x=-2\) and \(y=1\). The point satisfies both original equations.

blocks.html: A centre lying on a normal supplies the correct direction, but a specified circle must also have the correct radius and contain the point. Check every real contact value and reject any zero-radius construction.

sections.title: What if a tangent or radius is horizontal or vertical?
sections.label: Zero and undefined gradients
sections.intro: Use the geometry directly when a line has zero gradient or no finite gradient. The negative-reciprocal rule applies only when the starting gradient is finite and nonzero.

blocks.html:
• Horizontal curve tangent: \(y=f(a)\); vertical normal: \(x=a\).
  • Vertical circle radius: horizontal tangent through the contact.
  • Horizontal circle radius: vertical tangent through the contact.

A vertical tangent has no finite gradient. Its horizontal normal can still be written directly.

blocks.title: A horizontal radius gives a vertical tangent
blocks.prompt: For the circle \((x+2)^2+(y-3)^2=16\), find the tangent and normal at \(P=(2,3)\).
blocks.hint: The centre and the point have the same height. Sketch the radius before trying to use any gradient formula.
blocks.solution:
1. The centre is \((-2,3)\), and the radius to \((2,3)\) is horizontal. Its length is \(4\), so the point is on the circle.

  2. The tangent is perpendicular to this radius and passes through \(P\), giving \(x=2\). The normal is the radius line \(y=3\).

  3. A vertical tangent has no finite gradient; it should not be represented by a numerical negative reciprocal of zero.

blocks.html: Do not assign a numerical value to \(-\frac{1}{0}\). Write the vertical or horizontal line equation from its direction and the known contact coordinates.

sections.title: Why is squared distance easier to minimise?
sections.label: Build a distance function
sections.intro: Let \(P=(t,f(t))\) move on the allowed part of a curve, and let \(A=(u,v)\) be fixed. The square root is increasing on nonnegative values, so the same point minimises the distance and its square.

blocks.html:
\[D(t)=(t-u)^2+(f(t)-v)^2,\qquad d(t)=\sqrt{D(t)}.\]

State the allowed interval for \(t\), minimise \(D\), and then take the square root if the question asks for distance. Use the original curve to recover the other point coordinate.

1. For \(A=\left(0,\frac54\right)\) and \(P=(t,t^2),\quad0\le t\le2\), minimise the squared distance.\[D=AP^2=t^2+\left(t^2-\frac54\right)^2=\left(t^2-\frac34\right)^2+1.\]
  2. Equality holds at \(t=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\). The negative candidate is outside the interval.
  3. At the included endpoints, \(D(0)=\frac{25}{16}\) and \(D(2)=\frac{185}{16}\). The global minimum distance is \(\sqrt1=1\).

For \(A=(0,\frac{5}{4})\) and \(0\le t\le2\), the bound \(D=(t^2-\frac{3}{4})^2+1\ge1\) is attained at \(t=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\).

blocks.title: Minimise the squared distance and then take the square root
blocks.prompt: A point \(P=(t,t^2)\), with \(0\le t\le1\), moves along a parabola. Find the point nearest to \(A=(0,\frac{3}{4})\) and the minimum distance.
blocks.hint: Use \(D(t)=t^2+(t^2-\frac{3}{4})^2\). Filter stationary inputs by the allowed interval and compare the endpoint values.
blocks.solution:
1. \[D(t)=t^4-\frac{t^2}{2}+\frac{9}{16},\qquad D^{\prime}(t)=t(4t^2-1).\]

  2. The derivative vanishes at \(t=0\) and \(t=\pm\frac{1}{2}\). The negative value is excluded.

  3. \[D(0)=\frac{9}{16},\qquad D\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{2},\qquad D(1)=\frac{17}{16}.\]
  4. \[P=\left(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4}\right),\qquad d_{\min}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\]

blocks.html:
At a distinct interior nearest point on a smooth curve, the segment to the fixed point is normal to the curve. This follows from

\[D^{\prime}(t)=2(t-u)+2(f(t)-v)f^{\prime}(t)=0.\]

An endpoint minimum need not satisfy this normal condition.
Report everything requested: the allowed input, the full nearest point and the actual distance. A value of \(D\) alone is a squared distance.

sections.title: How do I know the nearest point really exists?
sections.label: Global comparisons and endpoints
sections.intro: A stationary point is only a possible answer. On a closed interval where the distance is continuous, compare all allowed stationary values with both endpoint values and any defined points where the derivative does not exist. Keep all points tied for the least value.

blocks.title: Changing endpoint inclusion can remove the nearest point
blocks.prompt: Let \(P=(t,t+2)\). Find the point on \(2\le t\le4\) nearest to the origin and its distance. Does a nearest point still exist if the interval is changed to \(2<t\le4\)?

fields.label: Nearest point on the closed interval
Minimum distance on the closed interval
Nearest point on the changed interval?

options.no: No; the lower bound is approached but not attained.
options.same: Yes; the same endpoint is still available.
options.right: Yes; the right endpoint becomes nearest.

blocks.hint: The squared distance is \(t^2+(t+2)^2\). Check its derivative on the actual interval.
blocks.solution:
1. \[D(t)=2t^2+4t+4,\qquad D^{\prime}(t)=4t+4>0\quad\text{for }t\ge2.\]

  2. On the closed interval the minimum occurs at \(t=2\), giving \(P=(2,4)\) and distance \(\sqrt{20}=2\sqrt{5}\).

  3. On \(2<t\le4\), every distance is larger than \(2\sqrt{5}\), but distances approach that value as \(t\) approaches \(2\) from above. No allowed point attains it.

blocks.html: On an open or unbounded domain, examine the relevant boundary limits as well. A limiting value is not automatically attained. State separately the lower bound and whether any allowed point reaches it.

Do not keep an unrestricted minimiser outside the given interval, or turn an excluded endpoint into a nearest point. A positive second derivative at one stationary point proves a local minimum; a global claim also needs the allowed domain checked.

glossary.definition: The point on the original curve where the stated tangent touches.
The line through the contact point perpendicular to its tangent.
A line that crosses a circle at two distinct points.
A single algebraic input counted twice; for line-circle substitution it identifies tangency.
The sum of the squared horizontal and vertical coordinate differences.
The smallest value attained over the entire allowed domain.
The greatest lower bound; it may be approached without being attained.

examples.title: Check a common contact using calculus and circle geometry
examples.question: The point \(P=(2,4)\) is claimed to be a common contact of \(y=x^2\) and the circle \((x-6)^2+(y-3)^2=17\). Verify the point, find the common tangent and normal, and confirm the line-circle contact algebraically.
solution:
First check both original equations:

\[4=2^2,\qquad(2-6)^2+(4-3)^2=16+1=17.\]
\[f^{\prime}(x)=2x,\qquad m_T=f^{\prime}(2)=4.\]
\[y-4=4(x-2)\Longrightarrow y=4x-4.\]

The circle centre is \(C=(6,3)\), and its radius to \(P\) has gradient

\[m_{CP}=\frac{4-3}{2-6}=-\frac{1}{4}.\]

This is perpendicular to the curve tangent, so the same line is tangent to the circle at \(P\).

\[y-4=-\frac{1}{4}(x-2)\Longrightarrow x+4y=18.\]

This common normal contains the centre, since \(6+4(3)=18\).

Substitute the tangent into the circle:

\[(x-6)^2+(4x-7)^2=17\Longrightarrow17(x-2)^2=0.\]
The repeated input \(2\) gives height \(4\), confirming the same single line-circle contact.

examples.title: An unknown contact point must have its normal through the centre
examples.question: A circle with centre \((5,0)\) shares a tangent with \(y=x^2+1\) at an unknown point \(P=(a,a^2+1)\). Find every possible contact, the circle equation and the common tangent.
solution: The tangent gradient is \(2a\). If \(a=0\), the tangent is horizontal and the normal is \(x=0\), which does not contain \((5,0)\). Thus \(a\ne0\).

For a nonzero gradient, the centre must lie on the normal:

\[0-(a^2+1)=-\frac{1}{2a}(5-a).\]
The quadratic factor has discriminant \(2^2-4(2)(5)=-36<0\). Therefore the only real contact input is \(a=1\), giving \(P=(1,2)\).
\[y-2=2(x-1)\Longrightarrow y=2x.\]
The point lies on both curves, and substituting the tangent into the circle gives \(5(x-1)^2=0\). The positive radius and repeated contact confirm the construction.

examples.title: Handle horizontal and vertical lines directly
examples.question: The curve \(y=(x-3)^2+2\) and the circle \((x-3)^2+(y+1)^2=9\) meet at \(P=(3,2)\). Find their common tangent and normal there. Also find the circle tangent at \(Q=(6,-1)\).
solution: At \(P\), both original equations hold. The curve derivative is \(2(x-3)\), which is zero at \(x=3\).
The curve tangent is horizontal, \(y=2\), and its normal is vertical, \(x=3\).
The circle centre is \((3,-1)\). The radius to \(P\) is vertical, so its tangent is also \(y=2\).
At \(Q=(6,-1)\), the radius is horizontal and has length \(3\). The circle tangent is therefore \(x=6\), and its normal is \(y=-1\).
No division by a zero gradient is needed. A vertical line is written as \(x=\text{constant}\), not in the form \(y=mx+c\).

examples.title: Find a nearest point by comparing squared distances
examples.question: For \(P=(t,t^2)\), with \(0\le t\le2\), find the point nearest to \(A=(0,\frac{5}{4})\) and the minimum distance.
solution:
The squared distance is

\[D(t)=t^2+\left(t^2-\frac{5}{4}\right)^2=t^4-\frac{3t^2}{2}+\frac{25}{16}.\]
The possibilities are \(t=0\) and \(t=\pm\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). Reject the negative input and retain both endpoints for comparison.
\[D(0)=\frac{25}{16},\qquad D\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=1,\qquad D(2)=\frac{185}{16}.\]
\[P=\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\frac{3}{4}\right),\qquad d_{\min}=\sqrt{1}=1.\]

The completed-square form also confirms the global bound:

\[D(t)=\left(t^2-\frac{3}{4}\right)^2+1\ge1.\]

Equality occurs at the allowed point found above.

examples.title: The same curve can have an endpoint minimum or no nearest point
examples.question: Keep \(P=(t,t^2)\) and \(A=(0,\frac{5}{4})\), but first restrict \(t\) to \([1,2]\). Find the nearest point. Then decide what changes if the interval is \((1,2]\).
solution:
The previous interior minimiser \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) is outside both new intervals. For every \(t\ge1\),

\[D^{\prime}(t)=t(4t^2-3)>0.\]

On the closed interval, the squared distance is least at \(t=1\):

\[P=(1,1),\qquad D(1)=\frac{17}{16},\qquad d_{\min}=\frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}.\]

On \((1,2]\), the input \(1\) is excluded. Every allowed point has a greater distance, while

\[d(t)\longrightarrow\frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\quad\text{as }t\longrightarrow1^+.\]
No nearest point exists on the open-ended interval. The greatest lower bound is \(\frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}\), but it is not attained.

extraPractice.title: Match a derivative to a circle radius
extraPractice.prompt: The curve is \(y=x^2+2x\). Find its tangent and normal at \(P=(1,3)\), writing each as \(y=mx+c\). Show that a circle with centre \(C=(-3,4)\) can share this tangent at \(P\), and find its squared radius.
extraPractice.hint: Check the contact point in the curve, then differentiate. The circle radius must lie along the normal through the contact point.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f(1)=3,\qquad f^{\prime}(x)=2x+2,\qquad f^{\prime}(1)=4.\]
  2. \[y-3=4(x-1)\Longrightarrow y=4x-1.\]
  3. \[y-3=-\frac{1}{4}(x-1)\Longrightarrow y=-\frac{x}{4}+\frac{13}{4}.\]
  4. \[m_{CP}=\frac{3-4}{1-(-3)}=-\frac{1}{4},\qquad CP^2=4^2+(-1)^2=17.\]

  5. The required circle is \((x+3)^2+(y-4)^2=17\). It contains \(P\), and its radius there is perpendicular to the curve tangent.

  6. \[y=4x-1:\quad(x+3)^2+(4x-5)^2-17=17(x-1)^2=0.\]

  7. The repeated intersection verifies that the line contacts the circle exactly at \(P\).

extraPractice.title: Treat a horizontal tangent geometrically
extraPractice.prompt: The curve \(y=(x+1)^2+2\) has vertex \(P=(-1,2)\). Give the constant height of its tangent and the constant input of its normal. Find the squared radius of a circle centred at \((-1,-2)\) sharing this tangent at \(P\).
extraPractice.hint: A zero tangent gradient gives a horizontal line. Its perpendicular is vertical; do not divide by zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[f^{\prime}(x)=2(x+1),\qquad f^{\prime}(-1)=0.\]
  2. \[\text{Tangent: }y=2,\qquad\text{normal: }x=-1.\]

  3. The radius from \((-1,-2)\) to \((-1,2)\) is vertical with length \(4\). The circle is \((x+1)^2+(y+2)^2=16\).

  4. Putting \(y=2\) into the circle gives \((x+1)^2=0\), confirming the unique contact.

extraPractice.title: Find both parallel tangents to a circle
extraPractice.prompt: A circle is \((x-2)^2+(y+1)^2=25\). Find every value of \(c\) for which \(y=2x+c\) is tangent to the circle. Give exact values.
extraPractice.hint: Substitute the line into the circle and require the resulting quadratic to have a repeated root.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[(x-2)^2+(2x+c+1)^2=25\Longrightarrow5x^2+4cx+(c+1)^2-21=0.\]
  2. \[\Delta=16c^2-20\bigl((c+1)^2-21\bigr)=500-4(c+5)^2.\]
  3. \[\Delta=0\Longrightarrow(c+5)^2=125\Longrightarrow c=-5\pm5\sqrt5.\]

  4. For either intercept, the repeated contact input is \(x=-\frac{2c}{5}\), and the height is \(y=\frac{c}{5}\). These points satisfy the original circle and line equations. The two signs give the two parallel tangents on opposite sides of the centre.

extraPractice.title: Report the distance after minimising its square
extraPractice.prompt: A point \(P=(t,t^2)\), with \(t\ge0\), lies on a parabola. Find the point nearest to \(A=(0,2)\) and its distance from \(A\).

retry.feedback: This is the least squared distance. Take its positive square root to obtain the distance.

extraPractice.hint: Minimise \(Q(t)=AP^2\). Justify the result on the whole nonnegative domain, then take the positive square root.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[Q(t)=t^2+(t^2-2)^2=t^4-3t^2+4.\]
  2. \[Q^{\prime}(t)=2t(2t^2-3)=0\Longrightarrow t=0\text{ or }t=\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\quad(t\ge0).\]

  3. On the positive domain the derivative is negative before \(\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\) and positive after it. The endpoint gives \(Q(0)=4\), while \(Q\) tends to infinity as \(t\) increases without bound.

  4. \[Q\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{2}\right)=\frac{7}{4},\qquad P=\left(\frac{\sqrt6}{2},\frac{3}{2}\right),\qquad AP=\frac{\sqrt7}{2}.\]

extraPractice.title: An excluded endpoint does not give a nearest point
extraPractice.prompt: A point \(P=(t,t^2)\) is restricted to \(0<t<1\). Consider its distance from the origin. Find the greatest lower bound of the distance, meaning the value it can approach but never go below. Give the complete set of inputs at which a minimum distance is attained.

retry.feedback: The input zero is excluded by \(0<t<1\). It gives a limiting distance, not an attained minimum.

extraPractice.hint: Check whether the closest limiting endpoint actually belongs to the allowed domain.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[Q(t)=t^2+t^4,\qquad Q^{\prime}(t)=2t+4t^3>0\quad(0<t<1).\]

  2. The distance is strictly increasing and positive throughout the allowed interval. As \(t\) approaches \(0\) from above, the distance approaches \(0\).

  3. The lower bound is \(0\), but the input \(0\) is excluded. For every allowed input a smaller positive input gives a shorter distance, so no nearest point and no attained minimum exist.

starters.title: Recover an unknown point of common tangency
starters.question:
A circle with centre \(C=(\frac{3}{4},0)\) shares a tangent with the parabola \(y=x^2\) at \(P=(a,a^2)\). Find \(a\), the squared radius, and the tangent in the form \(y=mx+c\). You may use

\[8a^3+4a-3=(2a-1)(4a^2+2a+3).\]
starters.hint: The centre must lie on the normal at the contact point. Handle a horizontal tangent separately before using a negative reciprocal.
starters.solution:
1. If \(a=0\), the tangent is horizontal but \(CP\) is horizontal too, so this is impossible. If \(a=\frac{3}{4}\), the radius is vertical while the tangent has nonzero finite gradient, so this is also impossible.

  2. \[m_T=2a,\qquad m_{CP}=\frac{a^2}{a-\frac{3}{4}}.\]
  3. \[(2a)\frac{a^2}{a-\frac{3}{4}}=-1\Longrightarrow8a^3+4a-3=0.\]
  4. \[(2a-1)(4a^2+2a+3)=0.\]

  5. The quadratic factor has discriminant \(4-48=-44<0\). Thus the unique real contact input is \(a=\frac{1}{2}\), giving \(P=(\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{4})\).

  6. \[r^2=\left(\frac{1}{2}-\frac{3}{4}\right)^2+\left(\frac{1}{4}\right)^2=\frac{1}{8}.\]
  7. \[y-\frac{1}{4}=1\left(x-\frac{1}{2}\right)\Longrightarrow y=x-\frac{1}{4}.\]

  8. The circle is \((x-\frac{3}{4})^2+y^2=\frac{1}{8}\). Substituting the tangent gives \(2(x-\frac{1}{2})^2=0\), verifying the stated contact.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: identify the derivative tangent gradient.
  • 1 mark: handle exceptional horizontal or vertical radius cases correctly.
  • 1 mark: impose the radius–tangent perpendicular condition.
  • 1 mark: obtain the stated cubic.
  • 1 mark: find the unique real contact input.
  • 1 mark: find the positive squared radius.
  • 1 mark: obtain the complete tangent equation.
  • 1 mark: verify the contact in both original geometric objects.

starters.title: Keep both points attaining the same global minimum
starters.question: A point \(P=(t,t^2)\) is restricted to \(-2\le t\le2\). Find every point nearest to \(A=(0,3)\), the least distance, and justify that it is a global minimum on this interval.
starters.hint: The curve and distance are symmetric in the sign of \(t\). Keep both signs when they lie in the interval, and compare both endpoints.
starters.solution:
1. \[Q(t)=t^2+(t^2-3)^2=t^4-5t^2+9.\]
  2. \[Q^{\prime}(t)=2t(2t^2-5)=0\Longrightarrow t=0,\quad t=\pm\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}.\]

  3. All three stationary inputs belong to \([-2,2]\). At the endpoints \(Q(-2)=Q(2)=5\); at \(0\), \(Q(0)=9\).

  4. \[Q\left(\pm\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2}\right)=\frac{11}{4}.\]

  5. Comparing all stationary inputs and both included endpoints gives the global minimum \(\frac{11}{4}\) of the squared distance. It is attained at both symmetric inputs.

  6. \[P=\left(\pm\frac{\sqrt{10}}{2},\frac{5}{2}\right),\qquad AP_{\min}=\frac{\sqrt{11}}{2}.\]

  7. The sign choice changes the point, so both coordinate pairs are needed. The reported distance is the square root of the minimum squared distance.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: formulate the correct squared distance.
  • 1 mark: differentiate and find all stationary inputs.
  • 1 mark: keep both signs within the feasible interval.
  • 1 mark: evaluate both endpoints and the remaining stationary input.
  • 1 mark: justify the global minimum by the complete comparison.
  • 1 mark: state both nearest coordinate pairs.
  • 1 mark: take the positive square root to obtain the least distance.

revision.body:
A geometric claim needs the correct point, the correct direction and the correct allowed domain.

Collect and verify contact data

\[m=f^{\prime}(a),\qquad y-f(a)=m(x-a).\]

Check the point in every original equation. A circle tangent is perpendicular to its radius, so the centre lies on the curve’s normal at a common contact. Keep the circle radius positive.

Confirm circle tangency and exceptions

Substitute the line into the circle: two distinct roots mean a secant; a repeated root means a tangent. Recover and verify the contact coordinates.

For finite nonzero gradient \(m\), the normal gradient is \(-\frac{1}{m}\). A horizontal tangent has a vertical normal. A horizontal radius gives a vertical circle tangent; a vertical radius gives a horizontal tangent.

Minimise the squared distance

\[D(t)=(t-u)^2+(f(t)-v)^2.\]

For \(P=(t,f(t))\) and fixed \(A=(u,v)\), minimise \(D\) on the allowed domain. Solve \(D^{\prime}=0\), filter the inputs and compare relevant values. Recover the point and report \(d_{\min}=\sqrt{D_{\min}}\).

Check global attainment

Include closed endpoints and any defined points where the derivative is undefined. Keep every point tied for the global minimum. An interior normal condition does not apply automatically at an endpoint.

For open or infinite boundaries, inspect limits. If the lowest bound is never reached, state that no nearest point exists. An excluded endpoint remains excluded.
revision.checks:
• Point belongs to every original curve and the line?
  • Perpendicular direction and horizontal/vertical exceptions checked?
  • Squared-distance inputs filtered and global values compared?
  • Full point, actual distance and attainment stated?
revision.examTip: Full point, actual distance and attainment stated?

orig_cross_topic_revision_trig_sectors.description: Find every allowed angle, match it to the correct geometric region, and optimise a sector only within its feasible dimensions.

sections.title: How do I find every allowed trigonometric angle?
sections.label: All branches and transformed intervals
sections.intro: State the angle unit and interval first. An inverse-trigonometric calculator result gives one principal value, so use the graph, symmetry or periodicity to find every allowed branch. Check that a proposed sine or cosine value lies between \(-1\) and \(1\).

blocks.html:
Use a reference angle and the quadrant signs. Sine is positive in quadrants I and II, cosine in I and IV, and tangent in I and III; each is negative in the other two quadrants. Check axis angles directly.

Repeat the sine or cosine pattern every \(2\pi\), or the tangent pattern every \(\pi\), until the whole requested interval is covered. Retain allowed inputs and remove duplicate values.

For \(u=a\theta+b\) with \(a\ne0\), transform the interval for \(u\), solve there, then transform every solution back. Reverse the endpoint order if \(a<0\). If \(a=0\), test the constant equation directly.

blocks.title: Factor without losing a whole branch
blocks.prompt: Solve \(2\sin^2\theta-\sin\theta=0\) for \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\). Give all angles in radians.
blocks.hint: Factor out \(\sin\theta\), but do not divide by it. Solve both factors separately.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\sin\theta(2\sin\theta-1)=0.\]
  2. \[\sin\theta=0\Longrightarrow\theta=0,\pi,2\pi.\]
  3. \[\sin\theta=\frac{1}{2}\Longrightarrow\theta=\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6}.\]

  4. All five inputs belong to the stated closed interval and satisfy the original equation. The endpoints \(0\) and \(2\pi\) are distinct input values.

blocks.html: Factor an equation before dividing by \(\sin\theta\) or \(\cos\theta\); dividing can lose their zero cases. Keep included endpoints: \(0\) and \(2\pi\) are different inputs even though they represent the same direction.

sections.title: Which angle unit and boundary does the sector formula use?
sections.label: Radians, arcs and boundaries
sections.intro: Convert degree angles to radians before using the arc or sector-area formulas. Match the calculator mode to the unit used in a trigonometric calculation.

blocks.html:
\[\theta_{\mathrm{rad}}=\frac{\pi}{180}\theta_{\mathrm{deg}},\qquad s=r\theta,\qquad A_{\mathrm{sector}}=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta.\]

For a proper sector, \(r>0\) and \(0<\theta<2\pi\). Its perimeter is the arc plus two radii:

\[P_{\mathrm{sector}}=r\theta+2r.\]

blocks.title: Convert the angle before using the sector formulas
blocks.prompt: A sector has radius \(7\,\mathrm{cm}\) and angle \(90^\circ\). Find the angle in radians, arc length, sector area and sector perimeter.
blocks.hint: The sector boundary contains two radii as well as the arc.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\theta=90\times\frac{\pi}{180}=\frac{\pi}{2}.\]
  2. \[s=r\theta=\frac{7\pi}{2}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta=\frac{49\pi}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]
  3. \[P=2r+s=\left(14+\frac{7\pi}{2}\right)\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

blocks.html: At a full turn, the region is a complete disk: its boundary is the circumference \(2\pi r\), without two extra radial edges. The proper-sector perimeter model therefore excludes \(\theta=2\pi\). The zero-angle case is also degenerate.
An angle in radians need not contain \(\pi\): for example, \(2\) radians is a valid angle. Arc and perimeter results have length units; sector areas have square units.

sections.title: How do I distinguish a sector, a triangle and a segment?
sections.label: Match each angle with its region
sections.intro: For \(0<\theta<\pi\), two radii and their chord form a nondegenerate triangle inside the minor sector. The minor segment is the part between that chord and the minor arc.

blocks.html:
\[A_{\triangle}=\frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta,\qquad A_{\mathrm{seg}}=\frac{1}{2}r^2(\theta-\sin\theta).\]\[c=2r\sin\frac{\theta}{2},\qquad P_{\mathrm{seg}}=r\theta+c.\]

The area subtracts the triangle; the boundary adds the arc and chord. These minor-segment statements use \(0<\theta<\pi\). For a major region, identify the region or use its complement before calculating.

Both sectors have radius \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\). The equal sine values give the same triangle area \(\frac12r^2\sin\theta=\frac{9\sqrt2}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2\). The angles are both below \(\pi\), so both segments are minor.

Central angleSector areaSegment area
\(\frac\pi4\)\(\frac{9\pi}{8}\)\(\frac{9\pi}{8}-\frac{9\sqrt2}{4}\)
\(\frac{3\pi}4\)\(\frac{27\pi}{8}\)\(\frac{27\pi}{8}-\frac{9\sqrt2}{4}\)

Areas in the table are measured in square centimetres. In each plot the orange dashed chord separates the triangle from the blue segment.

With radius \(3\), the angles \(\frac{\pi}{4}\) and \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) give equal triangle areas but different sectors and minor segments.

blocks.title: A segment uses an arc and a chord
blocks.prompt: A minor segment has radius \(2\,\mathrm{cm}\) and central angle \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find its area and its boundary length.
blocks.hint: Subtract the triangle from the sector for area. For the boundary, add the arc to the chord, not to two radii.
blocks.solution:
1. \[A_{\mathrm{seg}}=\frac{1}{2}(2)^2\left(\frac{\pi}{2}-\sin\frac{\pi}{2}\right)=(\pi-2)\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]
  2. \[s=2\times\frac{\pi}{2}=\pi,\qquad c=2(2)\sin\frac{\pi}{4}=2\sqrt{2}.\]
  3. \[P_{\mathrm{seg}}=(\pi+2\sqrt{2})\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

blocks.html: A positive triangle area smaller than \(\frac{r^2}{2}\) gives two angles in \((0,\pi)\); the maximum triangle area gives only \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). Extra geometric information may select a branch. Keep the surviving angle paired with its own calculated area.

sections.title: How do I build a sector model with fixed perimeter?
sections.label: Eliminate one variable
sections.intro: Draw and label the boundary before writing its length. For a proper sector with fixed perimeter \(P>0\), the two radii consume part of the available length, leaving the rest for the arc.

blocks.html:
\[P=r(\theta+2),\qquad\theta=\frac{P}{r}-2,\qquad A=\frac{Pr}{2}-r^2.\]\[0<\theta<2\pi\Longleftrightarrow\frac{P}{2+2\pi}<r<\frac{P}{2}.\]

Substitute the perimeter relation before differentiating. The objective is now a quadratic in \(r\); no trigonometric derivative is needed.

1. The proper-sector perimeter is \(r\theta+2r=18\), with \(0<\theta<2\pi\). Thus \(\theta=\frac{18}{r}-2\) and \(\frac{9}{\pi+1}
  2. The area is \(A=9r-r^2=\frac{81}{4}-\left(r-\frac92\right)^2\).
  3. The interior maximum is \(\frac{81}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2\) at \(r=\frac92\,\mathrm{cm}\) and \(\theta=2\) radians. Both range endpoints are excluded.

For perimeter \(18\), the feasible radius interval is \(\frac{9}{\pi+1}<r<9\). The area \(9r-r^2\) reaches \(\frac{81}{4}\) at \(r=\frac{9}{2}\), with \(\theta=2\).

blocks.title: Check that the unrestricted vertex is a feasible sector
blocks.prompt: A proper sector has perimeter \(14\,\mathrm{cm}\), with \(r>0\) and \(0<\theta<2\pi\). Find the radius, angle and greatest possible area.
blocks.hint: Eliminate the angle using \(14=2r+r\theta\), then maximise the resulting quadratic in \(r\).
blocks.solution:
1. \[\theta=\frac{14}{r}-2,\qquad A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta=7r-r^2.\]
  2. \[A^{\prime}(r)=7-2r=0\Longrightarrow r=\frac{7}{2}.\]
  3. \[\theta=2,\qquad A=\frac{49}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

  4. The angle satisfies \(0<2<2\pi\), and

    \[A=\frac{49}{4}-\left(r-\frac{7}{2}\right)^2\le\frac{49}{4}.\]

    The bound is attained by an allowed sector.

blocks.html: The perimeter equation changes if the boundary contains a chord instead of two radii. Do not optimise the proper-sector model for a segment or a complete circle.

sections.title: What if the sector has an extra angle or radius restriction?
sections.label: Feasible maxima and endpoints
sections.intro: Translate every geometric restriction into the variable used in the objective function. A stationary point outside that interval is not an allowed answer. Since \(r=\frac{P}{\theta+2}\), increasing the angle decreases the radius when the perimeter is fixed.

blocks.title: An angle cap can move the optimum to a boundary
blocks.prompt: A sector has perimeter \(12\,\mathrm{cm}\) and must satisfy \(0<\theta\le1\) radian. Find the radius and greatest area. Would that greatest value still be attained if the requirement were \(0<\theta<1\)?

fields.label: Attained with the strict angle cap?

options.no: No; it is an upper bound that is approached but not reached.
options.yes: Yes; the same sector remains allowed.
options.vertex: Yes; use the unrestricted quadratic vertex instead.

blocks.hint: Convert the angle condition into a radius interval before checking the quadratic vertex.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\theta=\frac{12}{r}-2,\qquad0<\theta\le1\Longrightarrow4\le r<6.\]
  2. \[A=6r-r^2,\qquad A^{\prime}(r)=6-2r<0\quad\text{for }r\ge4.\]

  3. The largest area occurs at the included left endpoint:

    \[r=4\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\theta=1,\qquad A=8\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

  4. With \(\theta<1\), the radius must satisfy \(r>4\), so every area is less than \(8\,\mathrm{cm}^2\). It approaches that value as \(r\) approaches \(4\) from above, but no allowed sector attains it.

blocks.html: Compare allowed stationary values, included boundary values and relevant limits. If the best value occurs at an excluded boundary, it may be approached without being attained. State the radius, angle, area and whether the requested maximum exists.
Return to the original perimeter and angle conditions at the end. The same quadratic can describe several different feasible intervals, with different answers.

glossary.definition: An angle measure for which arc length equals radius multiplied by the angle.
One of the different angle choices that produce the required trigonometric value.
A region bounded by two radii and their chosen arc.
The straight line segment joining two points on a circle.
The region between a chord and its minor arc.
The values satisfying every geometric restriction in the model.
