examples.title: Transform the interval as well as the angle
examples.question: Solve \(\sin\left(2\theta-\frac{\pi}{6}\right)=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) for \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\).
solution:
Set \(u=2\theta-\frac{\pi}{6}\). Transform both endpoints:

\[-\frac{\pi}{6}\le u\le\frac{23\pi}{6}.\]

The sine is positive in the first and second quadrants. All solutions in this transformed interval are

\[u=\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{2\pi}{3},\frac{7\pi}{3},\frac{8\pi}{3}.\]

Undo the transformation for every value:

\[\theta=\frac{u+\frac{\pi}{6}}{2}.\]
All four values lie in the original interval and return the listed sine angles. Solving only one period of \(u\) would have missed two answers.

examples.title: Distinguish the arc, chord and sector boundary
examples.question: A sector has radius \(8\,\mathrm{cm}\) and central angle \(60^\circ\). Find its arc length, area, chord length and sector perimeter.
solution: \[\theta=60\times\frac{\pi}{180}=\frac{\pi}{3}.\]
\[s=r\theta=\frac{8\pi}{3}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad A_{\mathrm{sector}}=\frac{1}{2}(8)^2\frac{\pi}{3}=\frac{32\pi}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

Bisect the isosceles triangle formed by the two radii and the chord:

\[c=2r\sin\frac{\theta}{2}=16\sin\frac{\pi}{6}=8\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

The sector perimeter uses two radii and the arc:

\[P_{\mathrm{sector}}=\left(16+\frac{8\pi}{3}\right)\,\mathrm{cm}.\]
The chord is a different boundary. Replacing the two radii by the chord would give the boundary of a segment, not this sector.

examples.title: Equal triangle areas can produce different sectors and segments
examples.question: Two radii of length \(3\,\mathrm{cm}\) enclose an angle \(0<\theta<\pi\). Their triangle has area \(\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2\). Find every possible angle, pairing each with its sector area and minor-segment area.
solution: \[\frac{1}{2}(3)^2\sin\theta=\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{4}\Longrightarrow\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}.\]

The stated interval includes both the acute and obtuse branches:

\[\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\quad\text{or}\quad\theta=\frac{3\pi}{4}.\]

For \(\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}\),

\[A_{\mathrm{sector}}=\frac{9\pi}{8},\qquad A_{\mathrm{seg}}=\frac{9\pi}{8}-\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{4}.\]

For \(\theta=\frac{3\pi}{4}\),

\[A_{\mathrm{sector}}=\frac{27\pi}{8},\qquad A_{\mathrm{seg}}=\frac{27\pi}{8}-\frac{9\sqrt{2}}{4}.\]
All areas are in square centimetres. The triangle area is the same because the sines agree; the sector and segment areas differ because the angles differ.

examples.title: Eliminate the angle before differentiating
examples.question: A proper sector has perimeter \(18\,\mathrm{cm}\), radius \(r>0\) and angle \(0<\theta<2\pi\). Find its greatest area and the corresponding radius and angle.
solution: \[18=2r+r\theta\Longrightarrow\theta=\frac{18}{r}-2.\]

Use the proper-sector angle condition to restrict the radius:

\[0<\frac{18}{r}-2<2\pi\Longrightarrow\frac{9}{\pi+1}<r<9.\]
\[A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\left(\frac{18}{r}-2\right)=9r-r^2.\]
\[A^{\prime}(r)=9-2r=0\Longrightarrow r=\frac{9}{2}.\]

\[\theta=2,\qquad A=\frac{81}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

The radius is feasible and the angle is a proper-sector angle.

\[A=\frac{81}{4}-\left(r-\frac{9}{2}\right)^2\le\frac{81}{4}.\]

The upper bound is attained, proving the global maximum.

examples.title: Apply an extra angle restriction before choosing the maximum
examples.question: Keep the perimeter \(18\,\mathrm{cm}\), but now require \(0<\theta\le\frac{\pi}{2}\). Find the greatest area. What changes if the upper angle bound is strict?
solution: The unrestricted optimum has angle \(2\), which exceeds \(\frac{\pi}{2}\). It is not allowed under the new condition.
\[0<\frac{18}{r}-2\le\frac{\pi}{2}\Longrightarrow\frac{36}{4+\pi}\le r<9.\]

The lower radius bound is greater than \(\frac{9}{2}\), so

\[A^{\prime}(r)=9-2r<0\]

throughout the new interval. The greatest area is at the included smallest radius.
\[r=\frac{36}{4+\pi}\,\mathrm{cm},\qquad\theta=\frac{\pi}{2},\qquad A_{\max}=\frac{324\pi}{(4+\pi)^2}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

If \(\theta<\frac{\pi}{2}\), the lower radius endpoint is excluded. The same area is an upper bound approached as the angle increases towards \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), but it is not attained. There is then no greatest area.

extraPractice.title: Keep each sine branch paired with its sector area
extraPractice.prompt: Two radii of length \(6\,\mathrm{cm}\) form a triangle of area \(9\sqrt3\,\mathrm{cm^2}\). Its included angle satisfies \(0<\theta<\pi\). Find every possible angle and corresponding sector area. Enter ordered pairs \((\theta,A)\), with angles in radians and areas in square centimetres.

fields.label: Every pair of angle and sector area

extraPractice.hint: The triangle uses \(\sin\theta\), whereas the sector uses \(\theta\) itself. A positive sine value can give two angles in the stated interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\frac{1}{2}(6)^2\sin\theta=9\sqrt3\Longrightarrow\sin\theta=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}.\]
  2. \[\theta=\frac{\pi}{3}\quad\text{or}\quad\frac{2\pi}{3}.\]
  3. \[A=\frac{1}{2}(6)^2\theta=18\theta\Longrightarrow A=6\pi\quad\text{or}\quad12\pi.\]

  4. The pairs are \((\frac{\pi}{3},6\pi)\) and \((\frac{2\pi}{3},12\pi)\). Both triangles have the given area, but their sectors do not have equal areas.

extraPractice.title: Do not divide away the zero-sine solutions
extraPractice.prompt: Solve \(2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin\theta\) for \(0\le\theta\le2\pi\). Give every angle in radians.
extraPractice.hint: Move everything to one side and factor. Dividing by \(\sin\theta\) would discard an entire family of solutions.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\sin\theta(2\cos\theta-1)=0.\]
  2. \[\sin\theta=0\Longrightarrow\theta=0,\pi,2\pi.\]
  3. \[\cos\theta=\frac{1}{2}\Longrightarrow\theta=\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{5\pi}{3}.\]

  4. All five angles lie in the closed interval and satisfy the original equation. They are distinct inputs even though \(0\) and \(2\pi\) point in the same direction on a circle.

extraPractice.title: Use a chord for a segment boundary
extraPractice.prompt: A minor segment of a circle of radius \(5\,\mathrm{cm}\) is cut off by a chord subtending \(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) radians at the centre. Find its exact area and perimeter.
extraPractice.hint: The segment is the sector minus the isosceles triangle. Its boundary is the arc plus the chord, not the arc plus two radii.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[A_{\text{sector}}=\frac{1}{2}(5)^2\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{25\pi}{3}.\]
  2. \[A_{\text{triangle}}=\frac{1}{2}(5)^2\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{25\sqrt3}{4}.\]
  3. \[A_{\text{segment}}=\frac{25\pi}{3}-\frac{25\sqrt3}{4}\,\mathrm{cm^2}.\]
  4. \[\text{Arc}=5\frac{2\pi}{3}=\frac{10\pi}{3},\qquad\text{chord}=2(5)\sin\frac{\pi}{3}=5\sqrt3.\]
  5. \[\text{Perimeter}=\frac{10\pi}{3}+5\sqrt3\,\mathrm{cm}.\]

extraPractice.title: Prove the sector maximum is feasible
extraPractice.prompt: A proper sector has perimeter \(24\,\mathrm{cm}\), including its two radial edges, with \(0<\theta<2\pi\). Find the radius, radian angle and greatest area.

retry.feedback: The maximum occurs at two radians. A full turn is excluded by the stated proper-sector model.

extraPractice.hint: Eliminate the angle using the perimeter. Complete the square in the radius and check the resulting angle lies in the stated interval.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[24=r(\theta+2)\Longrightarrow\theta=\frac{24}{r}-2,\qquad\frac{12}{1+\pi}<r<12.\]
  2. \[A=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta=12r-r^2=36-(r-6)^2\le36.\]

  3. Equality is attained at \(r=6\,\mathrm{cm}\). The corresponding angle is \(\theta=2\) radians, which belongs to \((0,2\pi)\). Thus the global maximum is \(36\,\mathrm{cm^2}\).

extraPractice.title: An angle cap removes the unrestricted optimum
extraPractice.prompt: A sector has perimeter \(18\,\mathrm{cm}\), including its two radii, and its angle satisfies \(0<\theta\le1\) radian. Find the radius and angle giving the greatest area, and state that area.

retry.feedback: This unrestricted stationary radius gives an angle of two radians, outside \(0<\theta\le1\). Use the feasible radius interval.

extraPractice.hint: Translate the angle restriction into a radius interval before choosing a stationary point.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[r=\frac{18}{\theta+2},\qquad0<\theta\le1\Longrightarrow6\le r<9.\]
  2. \[A=9r-r^2,\qquad A^{\prime}(r)=9-2r<0\quad(6\le r<9).\]

  3. The area decreases across the feasible radius interval. Its greatest value is at the included lower endpoint \(r=6\,\mathrm{cm}\), corresponding to \(\theta=1\) radian.

  4. \[A=9(6)-6^2=18\,\mathrm{cm^2}.\]

  5. The unrestricted stationary radius \(\frac{9}{2}\) would give \(\theta=2\), which violates the angle cap.

starters.title: A reflex-sector constraint moves the maximum to a boundary
starters.question: A sector has perimeter \(20\,\mathrm{cm}\), including its two radial edges. Its angle is restricted to \(\pi\le\theta\le\frac{3\pi}{2}\). Find the radius and angle giving the greatest area, and express that area exactly.
starters.hint: The larger permitted angle gives the smaller radius. Check the radius interval against the unrestricted stationary radius.
starters.solution:
1. \[r=\frac{20}{\theta+2}\Longrightarrow\frac{40}{4+3\pi}\le r\le\frac{20}{2+\pi}.\]
  2. \[A=10r-r^2,\qquad A^{\prime}(r)=10-2r.\]

  3. Every feasible radius is less than \(5\), since \(\pi>2\) gives \(\frac{20}{2+\pi}<5\). Therefore the derivative is positive throughout the interval.

  4. The area is greatest at the largest permitted radius, \(r=\frac{20}{2+\pi}\), which corresponds to the included angle \(\theta=\pi\).

  5. \[A_{\max}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{20}{2+\pi}\right)^2\pi=\frac{200\pi}{(2+\pi)^2}\,\mathrm{cm^2}.\]

  6. The angle \(\pi\) describes a semicircle whose straight boundary is the two collinear radii together. It is valid here. The unrestricted optimum at angle \(2\) radians is outside the given interval.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form the correct perimeter relationship.
  • 1 mark: derive both feasible radius endpoints with the correct order.
  • 1 mark: obtain area as a function of radius.
  • 1 mark: differentiate and show that the derivative is positive throughout the feasible interval.
  • 1 mark: choose the included maximum-radius endpoint.
  • 1 mark: recover its permitted radian angle.
  • 1 mark: give the exact greatest area with correct units.

starters.title: Compare two complete designs with the same perimeter
starters.question: A proper sector has perimeter \(10\,\mathrm{cm}\), including its two radii. Its angle satisfies \(\sin\theta=\frac{1}{2}\), with \(0<\theta<\pi\). Find both possible designs. Enter ordered pairs \((\theta,r)\) and \((\theta,A)\), using radians, centimetres and square centimetres respectively. State the angle of the design with greater area and justify the comparison.
starters.hint: Both sine branches are needed. Because the perimeter is fixed, the two designs have different radii; compare their complete area expressions.
starters.solution:
1. \[\theta_1=\frac{\pi}{6},\qquad\theta_2=\frac{5\pi}{6},\qquad r=\frac{10}{2+\theta}.\]
  2. \[r_1=\frac{60}{12+\pi},\qquad r_2=\frac{60}{12+5\pi}.\]
  3. \[A_1=\frac{1}{2}r_1^2\theta_1=\frac{300\pi}{(12+\pi)^2},\qquad A_2=\frac{1500\pi}{(12+5\pi)^2}.\]
  4. \[\frac{A_2}{A_1}=\frac{5(12+\pi)^2}{(12+5\pi)^2}.\]
  5. \[5(12+\pi)^2-(12+5\pi)^2=576-20\pi^2>0,\]

  6. For example, \(\pi<4\) implies \(20\pi^2<320<576\). Both denominators and areas are positive, so \(A_2>A_1\). The design with angle \(\frac{5\pi}{6}\) has the greater area.

  7. In each design, \(r_i(2+\theta_i)=10\), and both angles satisfy the original sine equation and interval. Equal sine values alone would not justify an area comparison when the radii differ.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: find both permitted sine branches.
  • 1 mark: connect the perimeter to radius and angle.
  • 1 mark: find both radii.
  • 1 mark: find the first sector area.
  • 1 mark: find the second sector area.
  • 1 mark: keep each radius and area paired with its own angle.
  • 1 mark: justify which positive area is larger.
  • 1 mark: state the winning angle and verify both designs against the original conditions.

revision.body:
Keep every allowed angle paired with its own dimensions and areas.

Find all angles on the stated interval

Use reference angles, quadrant signs and graph symmetry. Repeat sine/cosine patterns every \(2\pi\), and tangent patterns every \(\pi\), over the required interval. Keep included endpoints and remove duplicate values.

For \(u=a\theta+b\), with \(a\ne0\), transform the interval and then every answer back. Reverse endpoint order if \(a<0\). Factor before dividing by a trigonometric expression.

Use radians and the actual boundary

\[s=r\theta,\qquad A_{\mathrm{sector}}=\frac{1}{2}r^2\theta,\qquad P=r\theta+2r.\]

Convert degrees by multiplying by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\). The perimeter model requires a proper sector: \(r>0\), \(0<\theta<2\pi\). A complete disk has circumference \(2\pi r\), without two radial edges.

Separate triangle and minor segment

\[A_{\triangle}=\frac{1}{2}r^2\sin\theta,\qquad A_{\mathrm{seg}}=\frac{1}{2}r^2(\theta-\sin\theta).\]\[c=2r\sin\frac{\theta}{2},\qquad P_{\mathrm{seg}}=r\theta+c.\]

Use these minor-region statements for \(0<\theta<\pi\). Angles \(\theta\) and \(\pi-\theta\) share a sine but usually give different sector and segment areas. At \(\frac{\pi}{2}\), the two branches coincide.

Optimise only over feasible sectors

\[\theta=\frac{P}{r}-2,\qquad A=\frac{Pr}{2}-r^2.\]\[\frac{P}{2+2\pi}<r<\frac{P}{2}.\]

Add every angle or radius restriction before choosing a maximum. Compare allowed stationary values, included boundaries and limits. An excluded best boundary gives an unattained bound. Check the final radius, angle, perimeter and units.
revision.checks:
• Correct angle unit and every interval branch included?
  • Each angle paired with its own area and dimensions?
  • Sector, triangle and segment boundaries distinguished?
  • Stationary value feasible and maximum actually attained?
revision.examTip: Stationary value feasible and maximum actually attained?

orig_cross_topic_revision_sequences_bino.description: Extract the coefficient numbers, apply the progression rule in the question, and check every parameter and term count against its original conditions.

sections.title: How do coefficients become sequence data?
sections.label: Coefficient values and term positions
sections.intro:
Extract the requested numbers before using a sequence rule. A coefficient does not contain \(x\). For a positive integer \(N\), write

\[(1+kx)^N=c_0+c_1x+\cdots+c_Nx^N.\]

blocks.html:
\[c_0=1,\qquad c_j=\binom{N}{j}k^j\quad(1\le j\le N).\]

The complete term is \(c_jx^j\). Read the constant directly, including when \(k=0\). For a nonunit first term, retain its power as well.

If the full coefficient list starts a sequence, \(c_0\) is its first term. If the question selects different coefficients, map their positions explicitly.

\[(2+x)^4=16+32x+24x^2+8x^3+x^4.\]
Power\(x^0\)\(x^1\)\(x^2\)\(x^3\)\(x^4\)
Coefficient\(16\)\(32\)\(24\)\(8\)\(1\)

If the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are the first two terms of an arithmetic progression, \(u_1=32\) and \(u_2=24\). The common difference is \(24-32=-8\), so \(u_3=32+2(-8)=16\). The coefficient of \(x^3\) in the expansion is \(8\).

The separate AP starts with \(c_1=32\) and \(c_2=24\), so \(u_3=16\). This differs from the next coefficient \(c_3=8\).

blocks.title: A coefficient is a number, and its position is a separate choice
blocks.prompt: In \((3-x)^3\), let \(c_j\) be the coefficient of \(x^j\). The numbers \(c_1,c_2\) are the first two terms of an AP. Find \(c_2\), the common difference and the third term of that AP.
blocks.hint: Expand first. Use the two specified coefficient values as the first two AP terms; the next AP term need not be the next coefficient.
blocks.solution:
1. \[(3-x)^3=27-27x+9x^2-x^3.\]
  2. \[u_1=c_1=-27,\qquad u_2=c_2=9.\]
  3. \[d=9-(-27)=36,\qquad u_3=9+36=45.\]

    The coefficient \(c_2\) is \(9\), while its binomial term is \(9x^2\). Also, \(u_3=45\) differs from \(c_3=-1\).

blocks.html: The parameter \(k\) inside a binomial is not automatically a GP ratio. It becomes the ratio only if the question says so or the coefficient relationships prove it.

sections.title: How do I test an AP or GP without losing zero cases?
sections.label: Differences, ratios and zero terms
sections.intro:
For three consecutive AP terms \(u,v,w\), equate the two differences. This works even when a term is zero:

\[v-u=w-v\Longleftrightarrow2v=u+w.\]

blocks.html:
For a GP, one finite real multiplier must work twice:

\[v=ur,\qquad w=vr.\]

If \(u\ne0\), use \(r=\frac{v}{u}\) and check the next multiplication. Then \(v^2=uw\) is an equivalent shortcut.

If \(u=0\), both later terms must also be zero. An all-zero sequence permits every finite ratio; a nonzero first term followed by zeros has ratio \(0\).

blocks.title: Check the recurrence when zeros appear
blocks.prompt: Which listed triple can be the first three terms of a GP with a finite real common ratio? Give that ratio. Then decide how many finite real ratios work for the all-zero sequence.

fields.label: Common ratio for the valid listed triple

options.any: Every finite real ratio works; it is not uniquely determined.

blocks.hint: A finite multiplier always sends zero to zero. Test the two successive multiplications, not just the squared-middle-term shortcut.
blocks.solution:
1. For \((5,0,0)\), the recurrence works with \(r=0\):

    \[5(0)=0,\qquad0(0)=0.\]

  2. The other triples require a zero term to be followed by a nonzero term, which no finite ratio can produce.

  3. For the all-zero sequence, \(0r=0\) for every finite real \(r\). Its common ratio is therefore not uniquely determined.

blocks.html: The condition \(v^2=uw\) alone can accept a false GP such as \((0,0,3)\). Also, dividing by a parameter before checking its zero case can remove a valid solution. Return to the original successive multiplications.

sections.title: How do I keep every valid parameter branch?
sections.label: Solve, check and pair the answers
sections.intro: Write the coefficient equations first, then apply the stated AP or GP condition. Keep both signs from an even-power equation unless a given restriction selects one. Check each value in the original condition.

blocks.html:
When the binomial exponent is unknown, it must be a positive integer. For \(N\ge2\), the first two nonconstant coefficients are

\[c_1=Nk,\qquad c_2=\frac{N(N-1)}{2}k^2.\]

Use both given equations to find \(N\) and \(k\). Check zero factors before dividing, and reject noninteger exponents. If \(N=1\), the \(x^2\) coefficient is zero.
For a nonzero GP, use \(S_\infty=\frac{a}{1-r}\) only after checking \(\lvert r\rvert<1\). Apply this test to each parameter branch. Keep each surviving parameter paired with its own ratio and sum.

blocks.title: Keep each parameter paired with its own sum
blocks.prompt: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^6\) is \(\frac{15}{4}\). A separate GP has first term \(2\) and common ratio \(k\). Find every possible \(k\), then give the pairs \((k,S_\infty)\).

fields.label: All possible values of the parameter

blocks.hint: There are two signs when solving for the parameter. Check convergence and calculate the sum separately for each sign.
blocks.solution:
1. \[\binom{6}{2}k^2=\frac{15}{4}\Longrightarrow15k^2=\frac{15}{4}\Longrightarrow k=\pm\frac{1}{2}.\]

  2. Both ratios have magnitude less than one, so both infinite sums exist.

  3. \[k=\frac{1}{2}:\quad S_\infty=\frac{2}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=4.\]
  4. \[k=-\frac{1}{2}:\quad S_\infty=\frac{2}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{4}{3}.\]

sections.title: Which sum formula applies, and what does the tail mean?
sections.label: Finite sums, convergence and signed tails
sections.intro:
Let \(a\) be the first term and \(n\) the positive integer number of terms included. For an AP with common difference \(d\),

\[u_n=a+(n-1)d,\qquad S_n=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\]

For a GP, start with \(u_1=a\) and use \(u_{n+1}=ru_n\). When \(r\ne0\), this gives \(u_n=ar^{n-1}\). If \(r=0\), the sequence is \(a,0,0,\ldots\).

blocks.html:
\[S_n= rac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\quad(r e1),\qquad S_n=na\quad(r=1).\]

For \(r e1\), subtracting \(rS_n\) from \(S_n\) gives \((1-r)S_n=a-ar^n\), which explains the formula. If \(a e0\), an infinite sum exists exactly when \(\lvert r vert<1\):

\[S_\infty= rac{a}{1-r}.\]

The all-zero sequence instead has sum zero for every finite ratio; handle it directly. If \(r=0\), every partial sum from the first onward equals \(a\).

Define the signed remainder to mean the sum still to be added after the first \(n\) terms:

\[R_n=S_\infty-S_n=\frac{ar^n}{1-r},\qquad\lvert R_n\rvert=\frac{\lvert a\rvert\lvert r\rvert^n}{\lvert1-r\rvert}.\]

Use these formulas when \(\lvert r\rvert<1\). The first omitted term is \(u_{n+1}=ar^n\). A negative remainder means the partial sum is above the infinite sum; absolute error ignores that direction.

1. Here \(u_n=6\left(-\frac12\right)^{n-1}\) and \(S_\infty=4\). For the signed tail \(R_n=S_\infty-S_n\),
  2. \[R_n=4\left(-\frac12\right)^n,\qquad |R_n|=\frac4{2^n}.\]
  3. The strict bound \(|R_n|<\frac14\) gives \(2^n>16\implies n>4\). The smallest integer is \(5\). At \(n=4\), the error equals the bound.

For \(a=6\) and \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\), the partial sums alternate around \(4\). The signed remainder is \(R_n=4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\), while its magnitude decreases.

blocks.title: Separate finite sums from signed remainders
blocks.prompt: An AP has first term \(5\) and common difference \(-3\). A different GP has first term \(4\) and common ratio \(-\frac{1}{3}\). Find the AP sum \(S_4\), the GP sum \(S_3\), the GP sum to infinity and its signed remainder \(R_3=S_\infty-S_3\).
blocks.hint: Write a few terms to check the signs. A negative signed remainder means the partial sum is above the infinite sum.
blocks.solution:
1. \[S_{4,\mathrm{AP}}=5+2-1-4=2.\]
  2. \[S_{3,\mathrm{GP}}=4-\frac{4}{3}+\frac{4}{9}=\frac{28}{9}.\]
  3. \[S_\infty=\frac{4}{1+\frac{1}{3}}=3.\]
  4. \[R_3=3-\frac{28}{9}=-\frac{1}{9}.\]

    The partial sum is too large by \(\frac{1}{9}\); the absolute error is positive.

blocks.html: Some questions define signed error in the opposite order, \(S_n-S_\infty\). Follow the order specified; it equals \(-R_n\) here. For an accuracy requirement, compare the absolute error with the bound.

sections.title: How do I prove the least number of terms?
sections.label: Strict bounds and the preceding integer
sections.intro: Translate an accuracy statement into \(\lvert R_n\rvert<\varepsilon\) or \(\lvert R_n\rvert\le\varepsilon\), using the stated inequality. Use powers, a table or a calculator to locate the first possible positive integer. Then check it and the preceding admissible integer.

blocks.title: Prove that your integer is the first one that works
blocks.prompt: A GP has first term \(8\) and common ratio \(\frac{1}{2}\). Find the least positive integer \(n\) for which \(\lvert S_\infty-S_n\rvert<\frac{1}{5}\). Give the absolute errors at this \(n\) and at the preceding integer.

fields.label: Absolute error at the preceding integer
Absolute error at the least working integer

blocks.hint: The infinite sum is \(16\), so the absolute tail is \(\frac{16}{2^n}\). Check consecutive powers of two.
blocks.solution:
1. \[S_\infty=\frac{8}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=16,\qquad\lvert R_n\rvert=\frac{16}{2^n}.\]
  2. \[n=6:\quad\lvert R_6\rvert=\frac{1}{4}>\frac{1}{5}.\]
  3. \[n=7:\quad\lvert R_7\rvert=\frac{1}{8}<\frac{1}{5}.\]

  4. The absolute tail decreases each time another term is included. Since the preceding integer fails, the least value is \(n=7\).

blocks.html: For a nonzero GP with \(0<\lvert r\rvert<1\), the absolute tail decreases as \(n\) increases. This makes the two consecutive checks a proof of minimality. With ratio zero, or an all-zero sequence, the tail is already zero after the first term.
State what \(n\) counts: it is the number of retained terms \(u_1,\ldots,u_n\). The first omitted term has index \(n+1\). An equality at the error threshold fails a strict inequality.

glossary.definition: The numerical multiplier of a power of \(x\); for example, \(24\) in \(24x^2\).
The power attached to a coefficient: \(c_0\) is constant, while \(c_2\) multiplies \(x^2\).
The place in a sequence, normally beginning with \(u_1\). The question determines which coefficient supplies that term.
The fixed amount added to obtain the next term of an arithmetic progression.
The fixed multiplier used to obtain the next term of a geometric progression.
The sum \(S_n\) of the first \(n\) terms.
The partial sums approach one finite value as more terms are included.
Here, \(R_n=S_\infty-S_n\). Its sign says whether the partial sum is below or above the infinite sum.
The nonnegative difference in size, \(\lvert S_\infty-S_n\rvert\), used to test accuracy.

examples.title: Use selected coefficients to start a new AP
examples.question: The coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) in \((2+x)^4\) are the first two terms of an AP, in that order. Find its third term and the sum of its first five terms.
solution:
Keep the powers of the first term when extracting the coefficients:

\[c_1=\binom{4}{1}2^3=32,\qquad c_2=\binom{4}{2}2^2=24.\]

\[(2+x)^4=16+32x+24x^2+8x^3+x^4.\]

The coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(24\); its complete term is \(24x^2\).

\[u_3=24-8=16.\]

This is a term of the separately defined AP. It need not equal the next coefficient in the expansion, \(c_3=8\).

examples.title: Reject a false GP created by a zero first term
examples.question: The constant, \(x\) and \(x^2\) coefficients of \((k+1)(1+2x)^2+3x^2\), in that order, are the first three terms of a GP with a finite real common ratio. Find \(k\) and the ratio.
solution:
\[(k+1)(1+4x+4x^2)+3x^2\]

gives the three coefficients

\[u=k+1,\qquad v=4(k+1),\qquad w=4k+7.\]

A GP must satisfy \(v^2=uw\), so

\[16(k+1)^2=(k+1)(4k+7).\]
\[(k+1)(12k+9)=0\Longrightarrow k=-1\quad\text{or}\quad k=-\frac{3}{4}.\]
For \(k=-1\), the triple is \((0,0,3)\). No finite multiplier can turn its second term into the third, so this value is rejected.

For \(k=-\frac{3}{4}\), the triple is

\[\left(\frac{1}{4},1,4\right).\]

Both multiplications use \(r=4\), so

\[k=-\frac{3}{4},\qquad r=4.\]

examples.title: Retain both solutions of an AP coefficient condition
examples.question: The constant, \(x\) and \(x^2\) coefficients of \((1+kx)^3\), in that order, form an AP. Find every real value of \(k\).
solution:
\[(1+kx)^3=1+3kx+3k^2x^2+k^3x^3.\]

The three numerical coefficients are \(1,3k,3k^2\).
\[2(3k)=1+3k^2\Longrightarrow3k^2-6k+1=0.\]

For either consistent choice of sign, the coefficients become

\[1,\quad3\pm\sqrt{6},\quad5\pm2\sqrt{6}.\]

The two successive differences both equal \(2\pm\sqrt{6}\). Both values of \(k\) satisfy the original AP condition.

examples.title: An even power gives two ratios and two infinite sums
examples.question: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^5\) is \(\frac{10}{9}\). A separate GP has first term \(3\) and common ratio \(k\). Find all possible pairs \((k,S_\infty)\).
solution: \[\binom{5}{2}k^2=\frac{10}{9}\Longrightarrow k^2=\frac{1}{9}\Longrightarrow k=\pm\frac{1}{3}.\]

Each ratio satisfies \(\lvert k\rvert<1\), so the infinite-sum formula applies to both branches:

\[S_\infty=\frac{3}{1-k}.\]
\[k=\frac{1}{3}\Longrightarrow S_\infty=\frac{3}{1-\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{9}{2}.\]
\[k=-\frac{1}{3}\Longrightarrow S_\infty=\frac{3}{1+\frac{1}{3}}=\frac{9}{4}.\]

The answers must remain paired:

\[\left(k,S_\infty\right)=\left(\frac{1}{3},\frac{9}{2}\right)\quad\text{or}\quad\left(-\frac{1}{3},\frac{9}{4}\right).\]

examples.title: Track which side of the infinite sum a partial sum lies on
examples.question: A GP has first term \(6\) and common ratio \(-\frac{1}{2}\). Find \(S_4\), \(S_\infty\), the signed remainder \(R_4=S_\infty-S_4\), and a formula for \(R_n\).
solution: \[S_4=\frac{6\left(1-\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^4\right)}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=\frac{15}{4}.\]

\[R_4=4-\frac{15}{4}=\frac{1}{4}.\]

The four-term sum is below the infinite sum.
\[R_n=\frac{6\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=4\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n.\]

For contrast, \(S_5=\frac{33}{8}\) and \(R_5=-\frac{1}{8}\): the five-term sum is above the infinite sum. The signed tails alternate, but

\[\lvert R_n\rvert=\frac{4}{2^n}\]

decreases.

examples.title: A strict bound can exclude an equality case
examples.question: Continue with the GP having \(a=6\) and \(r=-\frac{1}{2}\). Find the least positive integer \(n\) such that \(\lvert S_\infty-S_n\rvert<\frac{1}{4}\).
solution: \[\frac{4}{2^n}<\frac{1}{4}\Longleftrightarrow2^n>16.\]
At \(n=4\), the error is \(\frac{1}{4}\). Equality does not satisfy the strict bound.
At \(n=5\), the error is \(\frac{1}{8}<\frac{1}{4}\).
The absolute error halves with each extra term. All earlier positive integers give larger errors, so the least number of terms is \(n=5\). The first omitted term is then the sixth term.

extraPractice.title: Use coefficient numbers as the first two arithmetic terms
extraPractice.prompt: The coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) in \((1-3x)^4\), in that order, are the first two terms of a new arithmetic progression. Find these coefficients, its sixth term and the sum of its first six terms.
extraPractice.hint: The binomial index tells you which coefficient to extract. After extraction, use the separately stated progression rule.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[c_1=\binom{4}{1}(-3)=-12,\qquad c_2=\binom{4}{2}(-3)^2=54.\]
  2. \[a=-12,\qquad d=54-(-12)=66.\]
  3. \[u_6=a+5d=-12+330=318.\]
  4. \[S_6=\frac{6}{2}(a+u_6)=3(-12+318)=918.\]

  5. The signs belong to the coefficients themselves. The AP is a new sequence specified by the question; later AP terms need not equal later polynomial coefficients.

extraPractice.title: Retain both parameter values from an arithmetic condition
extraPractice.prompt: The constant, \(x\) and \(x^2\) coefficients of \((1+kx)^5\), in that order, form three consecutive terms of an arithmetic progression. Find every real value of \(k\).
extraPractice.hint: Extract all three coefficient numbers, then apply twice the middle equals the sum of the outer terms.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[c_0=1,\qquad c_1=5k,\qquad c_2=10k^2.\]
  2. \[2(5k)=1+10k^2\Longrightarrow10k^2-10k+1=0.\]
  3. \[k=\frac{10\pm\sqrt{60}}{20}=\frac{5\pm\sqrt{15}}{10}.\]

  4. Both values satisfy the original AP equation. No sign, convergence or other restriction was given to remove either one.

extraPractice.title: A necessary geometric identity can accept a false zero case
extraPractice.prompt: Let \(u,v,w\) be the constant, \(x\) and \(x^2\) coefficients of \((k-1)(1+x)^2+2kx^2\), in that order. They must form a geometric triple: there must be a finite real number \(r\) such that \(v=ru\) and \(w=rv\). Find every permitted \(k\) and its ratio.

retry.feedback: At \(k=1\), the triple is \((0,0,2)\). It passes the squared identity but cannot satisfy \(w=rv\) for a finite ratio.

extraPractice.hint: Use \(v^2=uw\) to find candidates, then check both original recurrence equations, especially when a coefficient is zero.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[u=k-1,\qquad v=2(k-1),\qquad w=3k-1.\]
  2. \[v^2-uw=4(k-1)^2-(k-1)(3k-1)=(k-1)(k-3).\]

  3. The algebraic candidates are \(k=1\) and \(k=3\). At \(k=1\), the triple is \((0,0,2)\). No finite ratio can send its second zero to the final \(2\), so this candidate is rejected.

  4. At \(k=3\), the coefficients are \((2,4,8)\). They obey \(v=2u\) and \(w=2v\), so \(k=3\) and \(r=2\).

extraPractice.title: An even-power coefficient leaves two convergent ratios
extraPractice.prompt: The coefficient of \(x^2\) in \((1+kx)^4\) is \(\frac{3}{8}\). A geometric progression has first term \(4\) and common ratio \(k\). Find every possible ratio and corresponding sum to infinity. Enter ordered pairs \((k,S_\infty)\).
extraPractice.hint: The coefficient determines \(k^2\), not its sign. Test convergence separately for both roots.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[6k^2=\frac{3}{8}\Longrightarrow k^2=\frac{1}{16}\Longrightarrow k=\pm\frac{1}{4}.\]

  2. Both ratios have absolute value less than \(1\), so both progressions converge.

  3. \[k=-\frac{1}{4}:\quad S_\infty=\frac{4}{1+\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{16}{5}.\]
  4. \[k=\frac{1}{4}:\quad S_\infty=\frac{4}{1-\frac{1}{4}}=\frac{16}{3}.\]

  5. Convergence does not require a positive ratio. The negative-ratio progression alternates in sign.

extraPractice.title: A strict error bound fails at equality
extraPractice.prompt: A GP has first term \(3\) and common ratio \(-\frac{1}{2}\). Let \(S_n\) be its first \(n\) terms. Find the least positive integer \(n\) for which \(|S_\infty-S_n|<\frac{1}{16}\), then find \(S_n\) and the signed omitted tail \(S_\infty-S_n\) at that index.

retry.feedback: At five terms the error equals the stated bound. The question requires a strictly smaller error.

extraPractice.hint: Use the absolute value for the error tolerance, but retain the sign when reporting the omitted tail. Check the immediately preceding index.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[S_\infty=\frac{3}{1+\frac{1}{2}}=2,\qquad R_n=2\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)^n,\qquad |R_n|=\frac{2}{2^n}.\]
  2. \[|R_5|=\frac{1}{16}\quad\text{fails the strict inequality},\qquad |R_6|=\frac{1}{32}<\frac{1}{16}.\]

  3. The absolute tails decrease strictly, so the least index is \(n=6\).

  4. \[R_6=\frac{1}{32},\qquad S_6=2-\frac{1}{32}=\frac{63}{32}.\]

  5. At odd indices the tail is negative, but its absolute value remains the approximation error. A negative signed tail by itself does not mean the error is small.

starters.title: Recover a binomial exponent before building a geometric model
starters.question: In \((1+kx)^m\), where \(m\) is a positive integer, the coefficients of \(x\) and \(x^2\) are \(12\) and \(60\). Find \(m,k\). A GP then has first term \(12\) and ratio \(\frac{1}{k}\). Find its sum to infinity and the least positive integer \(N\) for which the absolute omitted tail after \(N\) terms is less than \(\frac{3}{4}\).
starters.hint: The nonzero linear coefficient permits a ratio of the two coefficient equations. Keep the binomial exponent and the later term count as separate variables.
starters.solution:
1. \[mk=12,\qquad\frac{m(m-1)}{2}k^2=60.\]

  2. The quadratic coefficient is nonzero, so \(m\ge2\). Also \(k\ne0\).

  3. \[\frac{60}{12^2}=\frac{m-1}{2m}\Longrightarrow\frac{5}{12}=\frac{m-1}{2m}\Longrightarrow m=6.\]
  4. \[k=\frac{12}{6}=2,\qquad r=\frac{1}{2},\qquad S_\infty=\frac{12}{1-\frac{1}{2}}=24.\]
  5. \[|R_N|=24\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^N.\]
  6. \[|R_5|=\frac{3}{4}\quad\text{does not qualify},\qquad |R_6|=\frac{3}{8}<\frac{3}{4}.\]

  7. The positive errors decrease strictly, so \(N=6\) is the least allowed count. Direct coefficient checks give \(6(2)=12\) and \(\binom{6}{2}(2)^2=60\).
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: form both coefficient equations.
  • 1 mark: retain the nonzero coefficient conditions and positive-integer exponent.
  • 1 mark: eliminate the parameter to find the exponent.
  • 1 mark: recover the parameter and check both coefficients.
  • 1 mark: identify the new ratio and justify convergence.
  • 1 mark: obtain the sum to infinity.
  • 1 mark: compare the exact errors at the proposed and preceding indices.
  • 1 mark: justify the least integer count, respecting the strict inequality.

starters.title: Convergence selects one algebraically valid arithmetic branch
starters.question: The constant, \(x\) and \(x^2\) coefficients of \((1+kx)^4\), in that order, form an AP. A GP with first term \(2\) and common ratio \(k\) has a sum to infinity. Find the permitted \(k\) and this infinite sum. Find the least positive integer \(N\) for which the omitted tail has absolute value less than \(\frac{1}{100}\).
starters.hint: First use the AP condition to find both parameter candidates. Then apply the stated infinite-sum condition to the separate GP.
starters.solution:
1. \[c_0=1,\quad c_1=4k,\quad c_2=6k^2,\qquad 2(4k)=1+6k^2.\]
  2. \[6k^2-8k+1=0\Longrightarrow k=\frac{4\pm\sqrt{10}}{6}.\]

  3. The plus root exceeds \(1\), so it cannot give the stated infinite sum for a nonzero first term. The minus root satisfies \(0<k<1\), so it is the permitted ratio.

  4. \[S_\infty=\frac{2}{1-\frac{4-\sqrt{10}}{6}}=\frac{12}{2+\sqrt{10}}=2\sqrt{10}-4.\]
  5. \[R_N=(2\sqrt{10}-4)\left(\frac{4-\sqrt{10}}{6}\right)^N>0.\]
  6. \[R_2=\frac{7\sqrt{10}-22}{3}\approx0.0453145>0.01,\]
  7. \[R_3=\frac{25\sqrt{10}-79}{9}\approx0.00632683<0.01.\]

  8. Since the ratio lies strictly between \(0\) and \(1\), these tails decrease strictly. Therefore \(N=3\) is the least count satisfying the error bound. The accepted parameter still satisfies the original coefficient AP equation.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: identify the three coefficient numbers.
  • 1 mark: form and solve the AP equation.
  • 1 mark: retain both algebraic candidates before checking convergence.
  • 1 mark: reject the divergent ratio and justify the retained one.
  • 1 mark: obtain the exact infinite sum.
  • 1 mark: form the omitted-tail expression.
  • 1 mark: check both the proposed and preceding term counts.
  • 1 mark: justify minimality using the decreasing positive errors.

revision.body:
Extract coefficient numbers, apply the specified progression rule, then check parameters and integer indices.

Keep coefficients separate from progression terms

In \((1+kx)^m\), with positive integer \(m\),

\[C_0=1,\qquad C_j=\binom{m}{j}k^j\quad(1\le j\le m).\]

The coefficient is a number; the term includes its power of \(x\). A new progression follows the rule stated in the question. Later terms need not be later polynomial coefficients.

Impose the original progression conditions

\[\mathrm{AP}:\quad2v=u+w.\qquad\mathrm{GP}:\quad v=ru,\quad w=rv.\]

For a GP, \(v^2=uw\) is necessary; check the recurrence when zeros occur. Do not divide by a possibly zero term. Retain every parameter branch until the original conditions select it.

Use sums with their conditions

\[u_n=a+(n-1)d,\qquad S_n=\frac{n}{2}\bigl(2a+(n-1)d\bigr).\]\[\mathrm{GP}:\quad S_n=\frac{a(1-r^n)}{1-r}\quad(r\ne1);\qquad S_n=na\quad(r=1).\]

For nonzero \(a\), an infinite GP sum requires \(|r|<1\) and is \(\frac{a}{1-r}\). A negative ratio can converge. If the first term is zero, the finite-ratio recurrence gives the all-zero sequence.

Separate a signed tail from the error

\[R_n=S_\infty-S_n=\frac{ar^n}{1-r},\qquad E_n=|R_n|\quad(|r|<1).\]

Use the absolute tail for an error tolerance. Test the proposed integer and its predecessor; equality fails a strict inequality. For \(0<|r|<1\) and nonzero first term, the errors decrease strictly. If \(r=0\), the tail is zero after the first term.
revision.checks:
• Correct coefficient indices and signs extracted?
  • AP/GP conditions checked, including zero cases?
  • All parameter branches tested for convergence and other restrictions?
  • Exact tail, strict inequality and least integer verified?

orig_cross_topic_revision_calculus_model.description: Recover the missing curve or amount, identify the region and variable, then distinguish a total quantity from its local rate of change.

sections.title: What must I recover before finding an area or volume?
sections.label: Gradient to curve, then to model
sections.intro: A gradient function gives how the height changes; it does not give the height itself. Integrate first, include the constant, and use the supplied point or level condition to determine it. Keep the original domain of the curve.

blocks.html:
\[f^{\prime}(x)=g(x)\Longrightarrow f(x)=\int g(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

The indefinite integral includes an unknown constant. For a power,

\[\int x^p\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{x^{p+1}}{p+1}+C\quad(p\ne-1),\]

on an interval where the expression is defined. Substitute a point into \(f\), and a gradient condition into \(f^{\prime}\). Check the recovered function against every condition.

blocks.title: Recover the constant before using the curve
blocks.prompt: A curve satisfies \(h^{\prime}(x)=3x^2-2\) and \(h(1)=4\). Write \(h(x)=x^3-2x+C\). Find \(C\), then find \(h(2)\).
blocks.hint: The point condition gives the height of the curve, so substitute into the integrated expression.
blocks.solution:
1. \[h(x)=\int(3x^2-2)\,\mathrm{d}x=x^3-2x+C.\]
  2. \[4=1-2+C\Longrightarrow C=5.\]
  3. \[h(2)=8-4+5=9.\]

    Differentiating the recovered expression returns the supplied gradient, and substituting \(x=1\) returns the supplied height.

blocks.html: The constant recovered in the curve changes its height and its later area or volume. Do not drop it because a new antiderivative constant will cancel in a definite integral. For example, integrating a constant height \(C\) over \([a,b]\) contributes \(C(b-a)\).

sections.title: Which curves and bounds define the required region?
sections.label: Intersections, order and geometric area
sections.intro: Sketch and label the region after recovering the curve. Use the stated vertical boundaries, or solve the boundary equations simultaneously to find their intersections. Retain only points allowed by the original domains.

blocks.html:
On an interval where \(U(x)\) is the upper boundary and \(L(x)\) the lower boundary,

\[A=\int_a^b\bigl(U(x)-L(x)\bigr)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

Check their order on each interval. If the order changes, split the integral and add the positive areas. For an axis-bounded region, split at sign changes: a signed integral can cancel positive and negative contributions.

blocks.title: Identify the actual region boundaries
blocks.prompt: Coordinates are in centimetres. Find the intersection inputs and the area enclosed by \(y=x^2-2x+2\) and \(y=2\).
blocks.hint: Equate the two heights, then check which boundary is above the other between the intersections.
blocks.solution:
1. \[x^2-2x+2=2\Longrightarrow x(x-2)=0\Longrightarrow x=0,2.\]
  2. \[2-(x^2-2x+2)=2x-x^2=x(2-x)\ge0\quad(0\le x\le2).\]
  3. \[A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,\mathrm{d}x=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\frac{4}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]

blocks.html: Keep the requested quantity visible beside the sketch. A stationary input solves \(f^{\prime}(x)=0\); an axis crossing solves \(f(x)=0\); a curve-line boundary solves \(f(x)=\ell(x)\). These equations answer different questions.

sections.title: How does rotating the region change the integral?
sections.label: Strip heights and squared radii
sections.intro: A vertical strip rotated about the \(x\)-axis forms a disk or washer. Radii are nonnegative distances to the axis. If the strip lies on one side of the axis, use the larger distance as the outer radius and the smaller distance as the inner radius.

blocks.html:
\[S(x)=\pi\bigl(R(x)^2-r(x)^2\bigr),\qquad V=\int_a^b S(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

A disk has \(r=0\). If a strip crosses the axis, its rotation is one disk with radius equal to the greatest distance reached; do not count overlapping disks twice. Split where the radius rule changes.

1. Integrate \(f'(x)=2x-4\) and use \(f(0)=5\) to get \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+1\).
  2. The strip has height \(5-f(x)\). Rotating it about the horizontal axis gives radii \(R=5\) and \(r=f(x)\). At \(x=2\), the washer area is \(\pi(5^2-1^2)=24\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^2\).
  3. \[A=\int_0^4[5-f(x)]\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{32}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]\[V=\pi\int_0^4[25-f(x)^2]\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{1088\pi}{15}\,\mathrm{cm}^3.\]

For \(f(x)=(x-2)^2+1\) below \(y=5\), the area strip has height \(5-f(x)\). Its rotation has washer area \(\pi\bigl(25-f(x)^2\bigr)\).

blocks.title: Rotate the region, not just its vertical gap
blocks.prompt: Coordinates are in centimetres. The region between \(y=2\) and \(y=x^2-2x+2\), for \(0\le x\le2\), is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find the washer area at \(x=1\) and the volume of the whole solid.

fields.label: Washer area at the stated input (cm²)

blocks.hint: Both boundaries are above the axis. The outer radius is \(2\), while the inner radius is the curve height.

blocks.html: A washer uses \(\pi(R^2-r^2)\), not \(\pi(R-r)^2\). The planar area uses heights, while the volume uses cross-sectional areas. Check square units for area and cubic units for volume.

For rotation about the \(y\)-axis, use horizontal strips: express the distances as functions of \(y\), integrate with respect to \(y\), and use the corresponding \(y\)-bounds. The same disk and washer reasoning applies.

sections.title: Does greatest volume mean greatest rate of growth?
sections.label: Accumulation and spatial derivatives
sections.intro:
For a continuous cross-sectional area \(S(x)\ge0\), define the volume accumulated from the fixed start \(a\) to a variable boundary \(k\):

\[V(k)=\int_a^k S(x)\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

After integrating in \(x\), the result is a function of \(k\). Differentiating that expression gives

\[V^{\prime}(k)=S(k).\]

blocks.html:
Maximise \(V(k)\) for the greatest accumulated volume. Maximise \(V^{\prime}(k)\) for the greatest increase per unit length. A nonnegative cross-sectional area makes the accumulated volume nondecreasing.

If \(k\) is in centimetres and \(V\) in cubic centimetres, \(V^{\prime}(k)\) has units of square centimetres. At a domain endpoint, interpret the spatial growth from the allowed side.

1. From \(r(x)=2-x\) and \(0\le x\le2\), integrate the disc areas up to \(k\).
  2. \[V(k)=\pi\int_0^k(2-x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi\left(4k-2k^2+\frac{k^3}{3}\right).\]
  3. Each slice below \(k=2\) adds volume because \(V'(k)=\pi(2-k)^2>0\). With \(V(0)=0\), the maximum accumulated volume is \(V(2)=\frac{8\pi}{3}\). The largest slice is at \(k=0\).

For radius \(2-x\), the spatial growth \(V^{\prime}(k)=\pi(2-k)^2\) is greatest at the start. The accumulated volume is greatest at the end, where \(V(2)=\frac{8\pi}{3}\).

A time rate needs a further relationship. If the boundary moves according to \(k=k(t)\), use the chain rule at the same instant:

\[\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}k}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{\mathrm{d}t}.\]

Without the boundary speed, a spatial derivative alone does not determine volume per second.

blocks.title: Convert a spatial derivative into a time rate only when justified
blocks.prompt: A solid has disk radius \(3-2x\) centimetres for \(0\le x\le\frac{3}{2}\), where \(x\) is measured in centimetres. Let \(V(k)\) be its volume from \(x=0\) to \(x=k\). Find the value of \(k\) giving the greatest volume, and \(\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}k}\) at \(k=1\). If a moving boundary has \(\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{1}{4}\,\mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}}\) at that instant, find \(\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}\).

fields.label: Spatial derivative at the stated boundary (cm²)

blocks.hint: The spatial derivative is the area of the next disk. A time rate additionally needs the speed of the boundary.
blocks.solution:
1. \[V^{\prime}(k)=\pi(3-2k)^2\ge0\quad\left(0\le k\le\frac{3}{2}\right).\]

    It is positive before the final endpoint, so the greatest volume occurs at \(k=\frac{3}{2}\,\mathrm{cm}\).

  2. \[V^{\prime}(1)=\pi(3-2)^2=\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^2.\]
  3. \[\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}V}{\mathrm{d}k}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{\mathrm{d}t}=\pi\times\frac{1}{4}=\frac{\pi}{4}\,\mathrm{cm}^3\mathrm{s}^{-1}.\]

blocks.html: Check the feasible boundary interval before choosing a maximum. Include its allowed endpoints. A zero derivative at one endpoint can coexist with the greatest accumulated volume there.

sections.title: How do I recover an amount from a changing rate?
sections.label: Initial amount, net change and extrema
sections.intro: Let \(q(t)\) be the signed net rate and \(Q(t)\) the amount present. If separate inflow and outflow rates are given, first form inflow minus outflow in matching units.

blocks.html:
\[Q(t)=Q(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^{t}q(s)\,\mathrm{d}s,\qquad Q^{\prime}(t)=q(t).\]

The integral is the net change. Add the initial amount to obtain the amount present. The letter \(s\) is the integration variable; \(t\) is the endpoint time.

If the question asks for total increase, integrate the net rate only over intervals where it is positive. Net change also includes the negative-rate intervals. These are changes in the amount present; separate gross inflow and outflow totals cannot be recovered from their difference alone.

blocks.title: Add the initial amount and check the time interval
blocks.prompt: A tank initially contains \(3\) litres. Its net rate of change is \(4-t\) litres per minute for \(0\le t\le6\), with \(t\) in minutes. Find the amount at \(t=6\), the greatest amount, the time at which it occurs and the total increase over intervals when the amount is rising.
blocks.hint: Integrate the signed net rate and add the initial amount. Compare the stationary time with both endpoints.
blocks.solution:
1. \[Q(t)=3+\int_0^t(4-s)\,\mathrm{d}s=3+4t-\frac{t^2}{2}.\]
  2. \[Q^{\prime}(t)=4-t=0\Longrightarrow t=4.\]
  3. \[Q(0)=3,\qquad Q(4)=11,\qquad Q(6)=9.\]

  4. The greatest amount is \(11\,\mathrm{L}\) at \(t=4\,\mathrm{min}\). The rate is positive before that time and negative afterwards. The amount stays nonnegative throughout the stated interval.

  5. The rate is positive only for \(0\le t<4\), so the total increase is

    \[\int_0^4(4-t)\,\mathrm{d}t=8\,\mathrm{L}.\]

    The later decrease makes the net change only \(9-3=6\,\mathrm{L}\).

blocks.html: A negative net rate means the amount is decreasing, not that the amount is negative. An amount can be greatest when its rate is zero. The greatest rate is a separate optimisation question.

For the continuous, differentiable models here, compare every allowed solution of \(q(t)=0\) with both included time endpoints. Retain every time if the greatest value is tied. Check the stated time interval and physical restrictions, such as a nonnegative amount; do not extend the model beyond them.

glossary.definition: The unknown constant retained when recovering a function from its derivative; a point or level condition can determine it.
An edge of the specified region, supplied directly or found where its defining curves meet.
The two-dimensional slice of a solid perpendicular to the direction used for integration.
A circular cross-section with a central hole; its area is the outer disk area minus the inner disk area.
The total built up from a fixed starting point to a variable endpoint.
Change with respect to a position or length, rather than with respect to time.
The signed rate after opposite contributions, such as inflow and outflow, have been combined.
The signed difference between the final and initial amounts.
The greatest value over the whole allowed domain, including every allowed endpoint.

examples.title: Recover the curve that will define the region
examples.question: A curve has gradient \(\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}x}=2x-4\) and passes through \((0,5)\). Find its equation and its least height.
solution: \[y=\int(2x-4)\,\mathrm{d}x=x^2-4x+C.\]

The point supplies a height condition:

\[5=0-0+C\Longrightarrow C=5.\]
The least height is \(1\), attained at \(x=2\). In particular, the whole curve lies above the \(x\)-axis.
Check both original facts: differentiating gives \(2x-4\), and at \(x=0\) the height is \(5\).

examples.title: Use the recovered curve to find a bounded area
examples.question: Coordinates are in centimetres. Find the area enclosed by the recovered curve \(y=x^2-4x+5\) and the horizontal line \(y=5\).
solution:
Find where the two boundaries meet:

\[x^2-4x+5=5\Longrightarrow x(x-4)=0\Longrightarrow x=0,4.\]

Between them, the vertical strip height is

\[5-(x^2-4x+5)=4x-x^2=x(4-x)\ge0.\]

The line is the upper boundary.
The limits came from curve-line intersections, not from setting the derivative to zero. The derivative zero at \(x=2\) locates the curve minimum, not a boundary of this region.

examples.title: The same region gives a washer integral after rotation
examples.question: Coordinates are in centimetres. Rotate the region between \(y=5\) and \(y=x^2-4x+5\), for \(0\le x\le4\), through one full turn about the \(x\)-axis. Find the volume.
solution:
Both boundaries are positive, and the region has a hole after rotation. Its radii are

\[R=5,\qquad r=x^2-4x+5.\]
\[V=\pi\int_0^4\left[25-(x^2-4x+5)^2\right]\,\mathrm{d}x.\]

Square the whole inner radius before subtracting:

\[25-(x^2-4x+5)^2=-x^4+8x^3-26x^2+40x.\]
A quick slice check at \(x=2\) gives \(R=5\), \(r=1\) and area \(24\pi\). Squaring the gap instead would give \(16\pi\), which is a different cross-section.

examples.title: Greatest accumulated volume is different from greatest growth
examples.question: A solid has disk radius \(2-x\) centimetres for \(0\le x\le2\), with \(x\) in centimetres. Let \(V(k)\) be its volume between \(x=0\) and \(x=k\), where \(0\le k\le2\). Find \(V(k)\), its greatest value, and where volume grows fastest per unit increase in \(k\).
solution: \[V(k)=\pi\int_0^k(2-x)^2\,\mathrm{d}x=\pi\left(4k-2k^2+\frac{k^3}{3}\right).\]

\[V^{\prime}(k)=\pi(2-k)^2.\]

This is cross-sectional area in square centimetres, or equivalently volume per centimetre of added length.

The derivative is positive for \(0\le k<2\), so volume increases to the final endpoint:

\[V_{\max}=V(2)=\frac{8\pi}{3}\,\mathrm{cm}^3.\]
The spatial growth \(\pi(2-k)^2\) decreases over this interval. Its greatest value is \(4\pi\,\mathrm{cm}^2\) at \(k=0\), interpreted from the allowed right-hand side.
At \(k=2\), the accumulated volume is greatest even though the final cross-sectional area is zero. The two questions maximise different functions.

examples.title: Recover an amount from a signed rate
examples.question: A tank initially contains \(7\) litres. Its net rate is \(6-2t\) litres per minute for \(0\le t\le5\), with time \(t\) in minutes. Find the final amount, the net change and the greatest amount during this interval.
solution:
Integrate the rate and include the initial amount:

\[Q(t)=7+\int_0^t(6-2s)\,\mathrm{d}s=7+6t-t^2.\]

\[Q(5)=7+30-25=12\,\mathrm{L}.\]

The net change is \(12-7=5\,\mathrm{L}\), not the final amount.

\[Q^{\prime}(t)=6-2t=0\Longrightarrow t=3.\]

The amount increases before this time and decreases afterwards.

Compare the allowed stationary time with both endpoints:

\[Q(0)=7,\qquad Q(3)=16,\qquad Q(5)=12.\]

The greatest amount is \(16\,\mathrm{L}\) at \(t=3\,\mathrm{min}\). The highest net rate instead occurs at \(t=0\), where it is \(6\,\mathrm{L\,min^{-1}}\). The amount remains positive throughout the modelled interval.

extraPractice.title: Recover the ordinate before finding the region
extraPractice.prompt: A curve has \(y^{\prime}=6x-6\) and passes through \((0,4)\). Write it as \(y=3x^2-6x+C\). Find \(C\), its stationary point and the area enclosed by the curve and \(y=4\).
extraPractice.hint: Use the point to determine the constant. Find the intersections before integrating the vertical separation.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[y=\int(6x-6)\,dx=3x^2-6x+C,\qquad y(0)=4\Longrightarrow C=4.\]
  2. \[y^{\prime}=0\Longrightarrow x=1,\qquad y(1)=1.\]

  3. Since \(y^{\prime\prime}=6>0\), \((1,1)\) is a minimum. Intersections with the line satisfy \(3x^2-6x=0\), giving \(x=0,2\).

  4. \[A=\int_0^2\bigl(4-(3x^2-6x+4)\bigr)\,dx=\left[3x^2-x^3\right]_0^2=4.\]

  5. The result is \(4\) square units. The derivative supplied the curve, but it is the recovered ordinate that determines the region.

extraPractice.title: Separate signed integral and total area
extraPractice.prompt: For \(f(x)=x^2-1\) on \([-2,2]\), find \(\int_{-2}^{2}f(x)\,dx\) and the total area between the curve and the \(x\)-axis.

retry.feedback: This is the signed integral. Split at the two zeros and add positive areas.

extraPractice.hint: The curve changes sign at two points. The total area adds the magnitudes of all three pieces.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[\int_{-2}^{2}(x^2-1)\,dx=\left[\frac{x^3}{3}-x\right]_{-2}^{2}=\frac{4}{3}.\]

  2. The curve is below the axis for \(-1<x<1\) and above it on the two outer intervals. Symmetry lets us calculate on the right half.

  3. \[A=2\left(\int_0^1(1-x^2)\,dx+\int_1^2(x^2-1)\,dx\right)=2\left(\frac{2}{3}+\frac{4}{3}\right)=4.\]

  4. The absolute value of the final signed integral would still be \(\frac{4}{3}\); it would not recover the cancelled area.

extraPractice.title: Use two distances from the rotation axis
extraPractice.prompt: The region between \(y=3\) and \(y=x+1\), for \(0\le x\le2\), is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find its volume.

retry.feedback: That squares the gap. Use the difference of squared radii: \(3^2-(x+1)^2\).

extraPractice.hint: The outer radius is \(3\), and the inner radius is \(x+1\). A washer has area equal to the difference of the two disk areas.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[V=\pi\int_0^2\left(3^2-(x+1)^2\right)\,dx.\]
  2. \[V=\pi\left[9x-\frac{(x+1)^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\pi\left(18-\frac{26}{3}\right)=\frac{28\pi}{3}.\]

  3. The answer is in cubic units. Squaring the separation \(3-(x+1)\) would create a different solid because it ignores the hole.

extraPractice.title: Largest cross-section and largest volume
extraPractice.prompt: A solid has disk radius \(\sqrt{4x-x^2}\) cm at position \(x\), measured in cm, for \(0\le x\le4\). Its volume up to position \(k\) is \(V(k)=\pi\int_0^k(4x-x^2)\,dx\). Find the position and area of the largest disk, and the position and value of the greatest accumulated volume.
extraPractice.hint: Maximise the disk-area function separately from the volume function. The volume keeps accumulating while disk area is positive.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[A(k)=V^{\prime}(k)=\pi(4k-k^2)=\pi\bigl(4-(k-2)^2\bigr).\]

  2. The largest disk is at \(k=2\) cm, with area \(4\pi\) cm\(^2\).

  3. \[V(k)=\pi\left(2k^2-\frac{k^3}{3}\right).\]

  4. Disk area is positive for \(0<k<4\). Therefore \(V\) increases throughout this interval and reaches its greatest value at the allowed endpoint \(k=4\).

  5. \[V(4)=\pi\left(32-\frac{64}{3}\right)=\frac{32\pi}{3}\ \text{cm}^3.\]

  6. Here \(V^{\prime}(k)\) has units of volume per unit length, equivalent to area. It is not a rate per second.

extraPractice.title: The final amount need not be the greatest amount
extraPractice.prompt: A tank contains \(4\) L at \(t=0\). Its net inflow rate is \(9-3t\) L/min for \(0\le t\le5\), with \(t\) in minutes. Find the net change over five minutes, the final amount, and the greatest amount and when it occurs.

retry.feedback: This is the net change. Add the initial \(4\) L to obtain the final amount.

extraPractice.hint: Add the initial amount after integrating the net rate. A negative net rate decreases the amount but does not make the amount itself negative.
extraPractice.solution:
1. \[Q(t)=4+\int_0^t(9-3s)\,ds=4+9t-\frac{3}{2}t^2.\]
  2. \[Q(5)-Q(0)=\frac{15}{2}\ \text{L},\qquad Q(5)=\frac{23}{2}\ \text{L}.\]

  3. The net rate changes from positive to negative at \(t=3\). Compare this candidate with both allowed endpoints.

  4. \[Q(0)=4,\quad Q(3)=\frac{35}{2},\quad Q(5)=\frac{23}{2}.\]

  5. The greatest amount is \(\frac{35}{2}\) L at \(t=3\) min. All amounts remain positive on the stated interval, so the model does not predict an empty tank.

starters.title: One recovered region, three different calculations
starters.question: A curve has \(y^{\prime}=2x-2\) and passes through \((0,3)\). The region enclosed by this curve and \(y=3\) is rotated about the \(x\)-axis. Find the enclosed area, the resulting volume, and the position and area of the largest washer cross-section.
starters.hint: Recover the curve first. The plane region uses the separation; the solid uses the difference of squared distances from the axis.
starters.solution:
1. \[y=x^2-2x+C,\qquad C=3,\qquad y=(x-1)^2+2.\]
  2. \[y=3\Longrightarrow x(x-2)=0\Longrightarrow x=0,2.\]
  3. \[A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\frac{4}{3}.\]

  4. Throughout this region the outer radius is \(3\), and the inner radius is the positive curve ordinate.

  5. \[V=\pi\int_0^2\left(9-(x^2-2x+3)^2\right)\,dx=\pi\int_0^2(-x^4+4x^3-10x^2+12x)\,dx.\]
  6. \[V=\pi\left[-\frac{x^5}{5}+x^4-\frac{10x^3}{3}+6x^2\right]_0^2=\frac{104\pi}{15}.\]

  7. The washer area is \(\pi(9-y^2)\). Since \(y\ge2>0\), it is greatest where \(y\) is smallest: at \(x=1\), where \(y=2\).

  8. \[A_{\mathrm{washer,max}}=\pi(9-4)=5\pi.\]

  9. The plane area and cross-sectional area have square units; volume has cubic units. They describe different geometric objects.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: recover the curve and its constant.
  • 1 mark: obtain both intersections and the correct upper boundary.
  • 1 mark: form and evaluate the enclosed-area integral.
  • 1 mark: identify the washer radii.
  • 1 mark: expand the volume integrand correctly.
  • 1 mark: obtain the exact volume.
  • 1 mark: justify the largest washer position using the positive minimum inner radius.
  • 1 mark: obtain the largest washer area and distinguish units.

starters.title: A local peak is not the global greatest amount
starters.question: A container has \(8\) L at \(t=0\). Its net inflow rate is \(3t^2-12t+9\) L/min on \(0\le t\le5\). Find the final amount, the greatest amount and its time, the least amount and every time it occurs, and the total increase accumulated over the intervals when the net rate is positive.
starters.hint: Integrate with the initial condition, find where the net rate is zero, then compare all candidates and both endpoints. The last part asks only for intervals with positive net rate.
starters.solution:
1. \[Q(t)=8+\int_0^t(3s^2-12s+9)\,ds=t^3-6t^2+9t+8.\]
  2. \[Q^{\prime}(t)=3(t-1)(t-3).\]

  3. The amount increases on \((0,1)\), decreases on \((1,3)\), then increases on \((3,5)\).

  4. \[Q(0)=8,\quad Q(1)=12,\quad Q(3)=8,\quad Q(5)=28.\]

  5. The final amount is \(28\) L. The greatest amount is also \(28\) L, at \(t=5\) min. The least amount is \(8\) L at both \(t=0\) and \(t=3\) min. The local peak at \(t=1\) is not the global greatest amount.

  6. \[\text{Total increase}=\int_0^1Q^{\prime}(t)\,dt+\int_3^5Q^{\prime}(t)\,dt=(12-8)+(28-8)=24\ \text{L}.\]

  7. The amount falls by \(4\) L between the two stationary times. Thus the signed net change is \(24-4=20\) L, which agrees with \(Q(5)-Q(0)\). The positive-part integral measures total increase during net-inflow periods; a net-rate model alone does not identify separate gross inflow and outflow.
starters.marking:
• 1 mark: integrate the rate and include the initial amount.
  • 1 mark: find both zero-rate times.
  • 1 mark: establish the three derivative signs.
  • 1 mark: evaluate the amount at both stationary times and both endpoints.
  • 1 mark: report the final amount and global greatest amount with its time.
  • 1 mark: report the global least amount and both times.
  • 1 mark: choose precisely the two intervals with positive net rate.
  • 1 mark: obtain their total increase.
  • 1 mark: distinguish total increase, net change and separate gross flows.

revision.body:
Name the target, keep its units and check the allowed domain.

Recover the curve, then identify the region

Integrate the derivative, retain \(C\), then use a point to determine it. Find intersections and check boundary order; split wherever it changes.

\[A=\int_a^b\bigl(y_{\rm upper}-y_{\rm lower}\bigr)\,dx.\]

A signed integral can cancel positive and negative pieces. Total area adds their positive magnitudes.

For rotation, measure radii from the axis

\[V=\pi\int_a^b\bigl(R(x)^2-r(x)^2\bigr)\,dx.\]

Radii are nonnegative distances from the axis. An axis-crossing strip gives a disk; split where the radius rule changes. About the \(y\)-axis use horizontal radii and \(dy\). Area has square units; volume has cubic units.

Accumulated volume and local cross-section differ

\[V(k)=\int_a^k A(x)\,dx,\qquad \frac{dV}{dk}=A(k).\]

Here \(k\) is a length, so \(V^{\prime}(k)\) is an area. Nonnegative slices make volume nondecreasing. The greatest volume and greatest slice can occur at different positions.

\[\frac{dV}{dt}=\frac{dV}{dk}\frac{dk}{dt}.\]

A time rate also needs the boundary speed.

Integrate a net rate and include the initial amount

\[Q(t)=Q(t_0)+\int_{t_0}^t r(s)\,ds,\qquad Q^{\prime}(t)=r(t).\]

The rate sign shows increase or decrease. Compare feasible stationary times and allowed endpoints, including ties. A local peak need not be the greatest amount. Net change is signed; total increase integrates only positive-rate intervals. Gross inflow and outflow need separate information.
revision.checks:
• Correct target: ordinate, gradient, area, volume, amount or rate?
  • Constants, intersections, domain and boundaries checked?
  • Radii measured from the rotation axis and squared separately?
  • Initial amount, all feasible extrema and correct units included?
